Lenders backing a $43 billion debt deal for Elon Musk -led Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) are reportedly trying to stop the company from sending valuable Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) AI chips into space, fearing they could lose the assets securing their loans.

Lenders fear they may not recover or resell the semiconductors if SpaceX launches them into space and subsequently defaults, the Financial Times reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the discussions. SpaceX says the financed chips will operate on Earth, and it remains unclear whether lenders secured the proposed restriction.

The dispute centers on "Project Saturn," a financing package that sold more than $30 billion in debt to institutional investors Thursday. Its largest component comprises $25 billion in investment-grade bonds backed by SpaceX's five-year chip lease payments, according to the FT.

The bonds reportedly offered yields near 8.3%, compared with approximately 7.2% on SpaceX's existing debt maturing in 2031. Although the new bonds mature in 2032, SpaceX will repay the principal within four years to limit creditors' exposure.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to Benzinga's request for comment.

The dispute reflects growing scrutiny of AI-related borrowing. Reuters reported last Monday that lenders were becoming more selective, while Goldman Sachs Research projected hyperscaler debt issuance could reach $420 billion in 2027.

Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers. The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips. SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter. It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents. The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating. The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class. SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips. The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people said. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday. The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added. More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco. Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX. SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s. Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus. The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease. “The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” said Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management. “This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he said. Additional reporting by Jill R Shah in New York.

( SPCX -7.69% ) sold $32 billion of bonds through a trust set up to buy Nvidia ( NVDA -14.01% ) chips on Thursday, with the largest piece paying investors a yield above 8%. And, according to reporting from The Financial Times, the lenders involved wanted guarantees that SpaceX would keep the financed chips on terra firma, apparently worried about the logistics of repossessing chips circling the Earth at about 17,500 mph. The stock was down 6.7% as of 11:39 a.m. ET on Friday as the whole market sees red. The bonds are part of a more than $40 billion financing package SpaceX announced in October. To try to keep the debt off its books, the financing runs through a separate entity -- a trust that sells the bonds, buys the chips, and leases them to SpaceX. Similar maneuvers are increasingly common across the AI data center market as companies look for ways to deal with ballooning debt balances . Functionally, however, SpaceX is still the one borrowing, and its quarterly lease payments are what pay the bondholders back. The largest piece, about $25.2 billion, was priced at a yield of 8.259%. The average yield on high-grade U.S. corporate debt was 5.95% that day, so investors are being paid about 2.3 percentage points more than usual for bonds that are supposed to be relatively safe. Bonds considered "junk" were yielding an average of 8.3% that day. The loans are secured by the chips in the same way your mortgage is secured by your home. If SpaceX ever defaulted, the lenders' fallback would be to repossess the GPUs and sell them. That's obviously quite difficult if they're in space. It's not clear if the lenders were able to get anything binding in the final documents, but SpaceX says these chips are for its "terrestrial compute build-out." President Vladimir Putin, meanwhile, vowed to retaliate against Ukraine for the “serious damage” it caused with three aerial attacks this week on the vital Kerch Bridge, which links illegally occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. “We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters in Shenzhen, China, where he attended the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Kushner and fellow U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff were in Berlin to reassure nearly 40 European leaders about Trump's discussions on ending the nearly five-year war at his trilateral talks with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Ukraine has long sought entry into NATO, particularly for its common defense guarantee under the alliance's Article 5, in which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, and whether Russia and Ukraine would ultimately accept them. The Berlin meeting was convened to explore Ukraine's postwar security arrangements with Kyiv's European backers. President Volodymyr Zelensky wants to ensure that Russia doesn’t invade again, and Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders. “I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” Kushner said. “And I think that that comes with at least what the Russians are saying, which is their intention is when this war is over to not have another war in the future.” Kushner said Trump is “open” to an Article 5-like security guarantee for Ukraine, although “obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that. And we also have to make sure that it’s part of a broader security package.” He stressed that Trump wants to make a deal with Europe “by his side,” and is not looking to impose a unilateral agreement. "Any deal we do will be in close consultation with Ukraine and with Europe. And that’s something that he also asked us to come here today and reassure people in that regard,” said Kushner, who is Trump's son-in-law. He and Witkoff have led Trump administration efforts to end the war that followed Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine. The most recent talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week yielded no major breakthrough. Trump called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, according to Kushner. Thursday's Berlin meeting came hours after the latest attack on the Kerch Bridge by Ukraine. The strikes have seriously damaged the 12-mile bridge over the Kerch Strait that links the Black and Azov seas. The span is vital to sustaining Russia’s military operations. The bridge is a potent reminder of Russia’s illegal annexation of the Crimean peninsula and has been a prime target for Ukraine. Train traffic stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti. The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Putin as he met in China with Xi and Trump, as well as to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable. In China, Putin insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered it closed to carrying military hardware or ammunition. Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section, which runs parallel to the road, is believed to be stronger in order to bear the greater weight of cargo transport. Roman Busargin said, and a drone killed a woman traveling by bicycle with her 8-year-old grandson in the Bryansk region, Gov. Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations. Explosions and sirens rang out across Kyiv during the day, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies sustained minor damage, officials said. Two people, including a 44-year-old woman, were killed and at least 23 people, including a 12-year-old boy, were reported wounded as Russian strikes caused damage in 12 regions. Russia’s bigger army hopes to exhaust Ukraine on the front line through sheer weight of numbers in terms of soldiers, armor and weapons. But Kyiv’s defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances. Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine’s resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv’s domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries. In China, Trump called Putin “my friend.” The American president’s relationship with Zelensky has soured recently, although the question of U.S. support for Ukraine could be raised by Democrats who will take control of Congress in January after their wins in the midterm elections. European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy as they fear being sidelined by Trump’s direct talks with Putin.

passages: U.S. envoy Jared Kushner has said Russia may accept NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine, adding that President Donald Trump wants to bring an end to Russia's full-scale invasion "with Europe by his side."

"I think we've got the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5," Kushner said alongside European leaders at a news conference in Germany on Thursday, referring to the part of NATO's treaty that enshrines the principle of collective defense.
It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, or whether Russia or Ukraine would accept them.
Russia's Foreign Ministry, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry and NATO were not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC on Friday morning.
Ukraine has long held ambitions to join the alliance.
Russia has previously said that if Kyiv joined NATO, it would cause problems for many years.
Russia launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on Ukraine's energy and transport infrastructure overnight, damaging three bridges in Kyiv and killing at least three people, authorities said.
They have led the Trump administration's efforts to end Russia's nearly five-year-long war with Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday described it as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved.

His comments come shortly after Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held historic trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a meeting that did not appear to result in any concessions on Ukraine or European security.

passages: BERLIN (AP) — U.S. envoy Jared Kushner on Thursday said Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war as it nears the five-year mark.

The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between Kushner, Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort and fear being sidelined by Trump's direct talks with Putin.

Kushner and Witkoff have led Trump administration efforts to end nearly five years of war following Russia's all-out invasion of its neighbor and recently have mediated new discussions, though the talks have yielded no major breakthrough.
The American leader called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said.
The meeting will also explore how Ukraine's European backers can fit into postwar security arrangements.
Kyiv wants to ensure that Russia doesn't invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders.

The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops.
It is a potent reminder of Russia's illegal annexation of the territory and has been a prime target for Ukraine.
Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations.
Explosions and sirens rang out across Kyiv during the day, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies sustained minor damage, officials said.

Russia's Foreign Ministry, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry and NATO were not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC on Friday morning.
Ukraine has long held ambitions to join the alliance.
Russia has previously said that if Kyiv joined NATO, it would cause problems for many years.

His comments come shortly after Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held historic trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a meeting that did not appear to result in any concessions on Ukraine or European security.

sources.title: YouTube Reportedly Nearing Multi-Billion Settlement With School Districts Over Social Media Addiction, Harms - AOL.co.uk
passages: The past few years have seen a surge in litigation against social media firms over addictive designs and alleged harms.

A group of social media companies including YouTube reached a settlement with Kentucky’s Breathitt County School District in May 2026 to avoid a trial, with YouTube shelling out a reported sum of more than $2 million.
Earlier this year, Meta settled with the attorneys general of dozens of states, some U.S. territories, and the District of Columbia over similar claims for up to $17.1 billion.
Both Meta and YouTube lost a California lawsuit in March 2026 to a young woman who claimed the sites caused addictive behavior, paying out $6 million.
Bloomberg reported Meta, TikTok and Snap are all defendants in the next school-district trial scheduled in the same consolidated federal case in Oakland, California, in February 2027.
The schools state that YouTube’s design forced them to take on additional costs like counseling and mental health programs for affected teenagers.

extraction.body: Google subsidiary YouTube is finalizing a settlement with school districts that have sued it over claims that the streaming giant deliberately designed YouTube to be addictive with no regard for mental health, Bloomberg reported on Friday. The payout could reach $3 billion, “people familiar with the matter” told Bloomberg, although it would be split between “thousands” of school districts. (If it were split equally among 3,000 districts, each would get $1 million before any deductions.) Bloomberg reported this would be the largest-ever corporate settlement with U.S. school districts. The reported deal also includes the introduction of new safeguards by YouTube. However, there’s no indication of what those safeguards are. $3 billion is less than 1% of Google owner Alphabet’s annual revenue, and tech companies have a long history of promising their sites are getting safer even as they are very obviously not to anyone paying attention. The ongoing litigation is a mass tort, which is like a class action, except the court weighs each plaintiff’s injuries and damages on an individual basis. The schools state that YouTube’s design forced them to take on additional costs like counseling and mental health programs for affected teenagers. extraction.body: Social media platforms Instagram and YouTube have a design defect which means they are addictive, a jury in the United States has ruled . The Los Angeles jury took nearly nine days to reach its verdict in the landmark case brought by a woman known as KGM against social media platforms. It awarded US$3 million in damages, with Meta (owner of Instagram) being 70% responsible and Google (owner of YouTube) 30%. The jury later awarded a further US$3 million in punitive damages. Both TikTok and Snap settled on confidential terms before the six-week trial commenced. This is Meta’s second big loss in the US courts this week, with a New Mexico jury finding the company guilty on March 24 of concealing information about the risks of child sexual exploitation and the harmful effects of its platforms on children’s mental health. KGM’s case is the first of its kind, but won’t be the last: it is one of more than 20 “bellwether” trials due to go to court soon. These are essentially test cases used to gauge juries’ reactions and set a legal precedent. As such, the verdict is set to have far reaching ripple effects. It could be big tech’s big tobacco moment, with thousands more similar cases waiting in the wings. KGM – now 20 years old – said she began using YouTube at age six and Instagram at age nine, and allegedly developed compulsive use patterns, including up to 16 hours in a single day on Instagram. The platforms’ design features, she argued, contributed to her anxiety, depression, body dysmorphia, and suicidal ideation. Her case argued that Meta and YouTube made deliberate design choices – for example, “infinite scroll” – to make their platforms more addictive to children in order to boost profits. It alleged the companies borrowed heavily from the behavioural and neurobiological techniques used by poker machines and exploited by the cigarette industry to maximise youth engagement and drive advertising revenue. These companies built machines designed to addict the brains of children, and they did it on purpose. Lanier cited an internal Meta study called “Project Myst”. This allegedly found that children who had experienced “adverse effects” were most likely to get addicted to Instagram, and that parents were powerless to stop the addiction. The moment [KGM] was locked into the machine, her mom was locked out. The jury heard that Meta’s internal communications compared the platform’s effects to pushing drugs and gambling. The jury found this internal awareness was the kind of corporate knowledge that supports liability. In addition, a YouTube memo reportedly described “viewer addiction” as a goal, and an Instagram employee wrote the company was staffed by “basically pushers”. Mark Lanier drew a direct parallel to tobacco litigation, arguing that where there is corporate knowledge, deliberate targeting, and public denial, liability follows. Meta argued KGM faced significant challenges before she ever used social media, and that the evidence did not support reducing a lifetime of hardship to a single factor. Meta’s lawyer highlighted KGM’s family dynamics as responsible for her mental health struggles, and argued social media may have actually provided a healthy outlet for her when she faced difficulties at home. Meta’s chief executive Mark Zuckerberg gave evidence for the defence: I’m not trying to maximise the amount of time people spend every month. On safety tools Meta added in recent years Zuckerberg said : I always wish we could have gotten there sooner. In closing arguments, YouTube’s lawyer argued there was not a single mention of an addiction to YouTube in KGM’s medical records. The companies centred part of their defence on Section 230 protections , arguing they cannot be held liable for content posted on their platforms. However, the judge instructed the jury that the way content is delivered is a separate consideration to what the content is. This limited Meta and Google’s ability to rely on Section 230 protections. This was one of the first cases against big tech which was a jury trial – something companies have previously been keen to avoid. For example, in June 2024, a few months ahead of a scheduled jury trial in the Department of Justice’s challenge to Google’s advertising technology monopoly, Google paid more than US$2 million (A$2.8 million) to the Department of Justice. This was treble the damages claimed, plus interest. In the US, a jury trial is only required when monetary damages are at stake. By paying the full damages amount upfront in that case, Google eliminated the damages claim and with it, the right to a jury. Until now, US courts have largely denied motions that focused on design. The effect of the jury’s verdict in KGM’s case is to demonstrate the limitations of the Section 230 protection. This is the first big tech case, on a global basis, that has examined addiction as a cause of damage. Other cases have focused on breaches of law. For example, in the case in New Mexico against Meta, the jury concluded the company made false or misleading statements and engaged in “unconscionable” trade practices that exploited children’s vulnerability and inexperience. It identified thousands of individual violations, resulting in a total penalty of US$375 million (A$539 million). KGM’s case paves the way for the many other actions seeking damages from social media platforms for the effects of addiction. There is logic for these cases to be heard concurrently in a class action in the US. The verdict could also be used as the basis for both class actions and individual actions on a global basis. Meta and Google have said separately they plan to appeal the verdict. Senior Research Associate in Media and Communications, University of Sydney Rob Nicholls is a part of the University of Sydney Centre for AI, Trust, and Governance and receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

extraction.body: Social media platforms Instagram and YouTube have a design defect which means they are addictive, a jury in the United States has ruled . The Los Angeles jury took nearly nine days to reach its verdict in the landmark case brought by a woman known as KGM against social media platforms. It awarded US$3 million in damages, with Meta (owner of Instagram) being 70% responsible and Google (owner of YouTube) 30%. The jury later awarded a further US$3 million in punitive damages. Both TikTok and Snap settled on confidential terms before the six-week trial commenced. This is Meta’s second big loss in the US courts this week, with a New Mexico jury finding the company guilty on March 24 of concealing information about the risks of child sexual exploitation and the harmful effects of its platforms on children’s mental health. KGM’s case is the first of its kind, but won’t be the last: it is one of more than 20 “bellwether” trials due to go to court soon. These are essentially test cases used to gauge juries’ reactions and set a legal precedent. As such, the verdict is set to have far reaching ripple effects. It could be big tech’s big tobacco moment, with thousands more similar cases waiting in the wings. KGM – now 20 years old – said she began using YouTube at age six and Instagram at age nine, and allegedly developed compulsive use patterns, including up to 16 hours in a single day on Instagram. The platforms’ design features, she argued, contributed to her anxiety, depression, body dysmorphia, and suicidal ideation. Her case argued that Meta and YouTube made deliberate design choices – for example, “infinite scroll” – to make their platforms more addictive to children in order to boost profits. It alleged the companies borrowed heavily from the behavioural and neurobiological techniques used by poker machines and exploited by the cigarette industry to maximise youth engagement and drive advertising revenue. These companies built machines designed to addict the brains of children, and they did it on purpose. Lanier cited an internal Meta study called “Project Myst”. This allegedly found that children who had experienced “adverse effects” were most likely to get addicted to Instagram, and that parents were powerless to stop the addiction. The moment [KGM] was locked into the machine, her mom was locked out. The jury heard that Meta’s internal communications compared the platform’s effects to pushing drugs and gambling. The jury found this internal awareness was the kind of corporate knowledge that supports liability. In addition, a YouTube memo reportedly described “viewer addiction” as a goal, and an Instagram employee wrote the company was staffed by “basically pushers”. Mark Lanier drew a direct parallel to tobacco litigation, arguing that where there is corporate knowledge, deliberate targeting, and public denial, liability follows. Meta argued KGM faced significant challenges before she ever used social media, and that the evidence did not support reducing a lifetime of hardship to a single factor. Meta’s lawyer highlighted KGM’s family dynamics as responsible for her mental health struggles, and argued social media may have actually provided a healthy outlet for her when she faced difficulties at home. Meta’s chief executive Mark Zuckerberg gave evidence for the defence: I’m not trying to maximise the amount of time people spend every month. On safety tools Meta added in recent years Zuckerberg said : I always wish we could have gotten there sooner. In closing arguments, YouTube’s lawyer argued there was not a single mention of an addiction to YouTube in KGM’s medical records. The companies centred part of their defence on Section 230 protections , arguing they cannot be held liable for content posted on their platforms. However, the judge instructed the jury that the way content is delivered is a separate consideration to what the content is. This limited Meta and Google’s ability to rely on Section 230 protections. This was one of the first cases against big tech which was a jury trial – something companies have previously been keen to avoid. For example, in June 2024, a few months ahead of a scheduled jury trial in the Department of Justice’s challenge to Google’s advertising technology monopoly, Google paid more than US$2 million (A$2.8 million) to the Department of Justice. This was treble the damages claimed, plus interest. In the US, a jury trial is only required when monetary damages are at stake. By paying the full damages amount upfront in that case, Google eliminated the damages claim and with it, the right to a jury. Until now, US courts have largely denied motions that focused on design. The effect of the jury’s verdict in KGM’s case is to demonstrate the limitations of the Section 230 protection. This is the first big tech case, on a global basis, that has examined addiction as a cause of damage. Other cases have focused on breaches of law. For example, in the case in New Mexico against Meta, the jury concluded the company made false or misleading statements and engaged in “unconscionable” trade practices that exploited children’s vulnerability and inexperience. It identified thousands of individual violations, resulting in a total penalty of US$375 million (A$539 million). KGM’s case paves the way for the many other actions seeking damages from social media platforms for the effects of addiction. There is logic for these cases to be heard concurrently in a class action in the US. The verdict could also be used as the basis for both class actions and individual actions on a global basis. Meta and Google have said separately they plan to appeal the verdict. Senior Research Associate in Media and Communications, University of Sydney Rob Nicholls is a part of the University of Sydney Centre for AI, Trust, and Governance and receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

sources.title: Bitcoin suffered identical sell-off pattern ahead of Anthropic, SpaceX IPOs — what happens next? - CNBC
passages: Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.
The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing.
"Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC.
"The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display.
Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market."
Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations.
Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next.
With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

"[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm.
Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole.

Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.

extraction.body: Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery. The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Ether declined 25.3% in the 30 days preceding Anthropic's debut, and 28% in the same window ahead of SpaceX. "Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC. "The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market." "Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash." While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment. Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns. "[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here." The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said. "Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable." Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000. As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35. Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand. Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said. "Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite." "The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin." The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Ether declined 25.3% in the 30 days preceding Anthropic's debut, and 28% in the same window ahead of SpaceX.

"Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC. "The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market."

"Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash."

While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment.

Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

"[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here."
The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said.

"Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable."
Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000.

As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35.

Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.

"Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite."

"The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin."

The listing has also coincided with a rebound in technology stocks and Nasdaq futures, improving risk appetite across financial markets. Bitcoin recovered toward $64,000 as equity futures strengthened, suggesting that sentiment surrounding the IPO could influence short-term crypto price action. However, the relationship remains uncertain. Bitcoin’s recent decline has also been driven by broader market deleveraging, institutional flows and macroeconomic concerns, meaning the IPO alone may not determine its direction. Holding above this area could allow $BTC to stabilize and attempt a recovery toward $65,000–$67,500. A sustained move above $67,500 would strengthen the short-term bullish outlook and potentially open the path toward $70,000. However, a breakdown below $62,000 could expose Bitcoin to further downside toward $59,000, followed by the $57,800 region, which represents a key previous low. Bitcoin’s pre-IPO decline has created a compelling comparison with the SpaceX listing, and Anthropic’s debut could provide a short-term catalyst for a recovery. Yet the previous cycle also showed that an initial rally can fade before the market establishes a durable bottom. Traders will therefore watch whether $BTC can hold $62,000 and regain $67,500 in the coming sessions. If history repeats, Bitcoin could see a relief rally, but the next move may not be as straightforward as bulls expect.

The company announced that it completed both its public and private offerings on the 20th.
The public offering consisted of 1.127 billion shares at $83 per share, totaling approximately $93.5 billion.
Including the private placement, the total funding reached approximately $119.5 billion.
According to CNBC, Bitcoin's price fell 22.7% in the 30 days prior to the Anthropic listing, and it dropped 22.3% in the month leading up to the SpaceX listing on June 12th.
Ethereum also saw similar selling pressure in the cryptocurrency market ahead of the two major IPOs, declining 25.3% and 28% during the respective periods.
He views Bitcoin as being in the early stages of forming a bottom and believes the market is likely to repeat fluctuations for the time being.
The timing of when lock-up periods on IPO-allocated shares expire could also impact capital flows.

The SpaceX IPO documentation includes a structure where share sale restrictions vary by existing shareholder, and some holdings become eligible for trading in stages following future earnings releases.
Analysts suggest that when large IPOs occur, the correlation across asset markets can rise sharply as investors sell existing assets to buy newly listed stocks.

Matthew Sheffield, Chief Investment Officer at Sharplink, cited the simultaneous sell-off of tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, and cryptocurrencies during the first 15 minutes of Anthropic's listing as an example of such capital movement.
He noted that even assets that function as stores of value in the long term are influenced by cash liquidity in the short term.

Other factors cited for the recent weakness in cryptocurrency include fund outflows from exchange-traded funds, the liquidation of leveraged positions, macroeconomic uncertainty, and risk-aversion sentiment.
Nicolai Søndergaard, a research analyst at Nansen, identified $60,000 to $62,000 as the next critical test range for Bitcoin.
However, he compared Bitcoin's recovery phase to "early spring" right after the end of deep winter, explaining that sharp cold snaps and rain could still occur during the rebound process.

passages: Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year.

With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public.
As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically.

The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations.
Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention.
If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return.

What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge.

extraction.body: Bitcoin and ether just traced the same sharp sell-off pattern that preceded SpaceX's blockbuster IPO earlier this year, raising urgent questions about whether institutional money is abandoning crypto for hot tech listings. With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public. The crypto market just delivered an eerie sense of déjà vu. Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year. The correlation is raising uncomfortable questions for crypto bulls about whether institutional money views digital assets as a liquidity source to fund allocations in hot tech IPOs. As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically. The pattern matches what happened in the lead-up to SpaceX's listing, when both cryptocurrencies shed double-digit percentages before finding support only after the IPO priced. When a massive IPO looms, institutional investors appear to be liquidating portions of their crypto holdings to free up capital for new allocations. It's a liquidity rotation that hits hardest in the two to three weeks before pricing, precisely when underwriters are locking in final commitments from large buyers. Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention. But here's where it gets interesting for crypto traders. After SpaceX priced its IPO, bitcoin and ether both stabilized within days and then mounted modest recoveries over the following weeks. coreStoryFacts.text: Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.
The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing.
"Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC.
"The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display.
Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market."
Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations.
Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next.
With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

"[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm.
Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole.

Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.
Bitcoin’s latest price decline is drawing comparisons with its pre-SpaceX IPO correction, raising speculation that history could repeat as Anthropic makes its public-market debut.
$BTC has dropped toward $62,000 after a sharp sell-off, closely mirroring the weakness seen before SpaceX’s IPO earlier this year.
After SpaceX went public in June, $BTC staged a short-term rebound, climbing from around $63,000 toward $66,000 over the following days.
Anthropic’s IPO has become a major market event, with the company pricing shares at $83, raising approximately $81.3 billion through its public offering.
Bitcoin has declined nearly 28% from its September peak near $87,400, with selling pressure intensifying ahead of Anthropic’s November 19 debut.
If history repeats, Bitcoin could see a relief rally, but the next move may not be as straightforward as bulls expect.
With Anthropic’s debut adding a fresh market catalyst, traders are now watching whether Bitcoin can stage another relief rally, or if the current sell-off has further room to run.
Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol 'ANT' on the 19th (local time).
The company announced that it completed both its public and private offerings on the 20th.
The public offering consisted of 1.127 billion shares at $83 per share, totaling approximately $93.5 billion.
Including the private placement, the total funding reached approximately $119.5 billion.
According to CNBC, Bitcoin's price fell 22.7% in the 30 days prior to the Anthropic listing, and it dropped 22.3% in the month leading up to the SpaceX listing on June 12th.

"Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash." While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment. Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns. "[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here." The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said. "Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable." As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35. Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand. Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said. "Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite." "The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin." Bitcoin recovered toward $64,000 as equity futures strengthened, suggesting that sentiment surrounding the IPO could influence short-term crypto price action. However, the relationship remains uncertain. Bitcoin’s recent decline has also been driven by broader market deleveraging, institutional flows and macroeconomic concerns, meaning the IPO alone may not determine its direction. Bitcoin’s immediate recovery remains fragile after the sharp decline toward $62,000. The $62,000 zone is the critical support level. Holding above this area could allow $BTC to stabilize and attempt a recovery toward $65,000–$67,500. A sustained move above $67,500 would strengthen the short-term bullish outlook and potentially open the path toward $70,000. However, a breakdown below $62,000 could expose Bitcoin to further downside toward $59,000, followed by the $57,800 region, which represents a key previous low. Yet the previous cycle also showed that an initial rally can fade before the market establishes a durable bottom. Traders will therefore watch whether $BTC can hold $62,000 and regain $67,500 in the coming sessions. If history repeats, Bitcoin could see a relief rally, but the next move may not be as straightforward as bulls expect.

sources.title: Bitcoin Mirrors SpaceX Pre-IPO Dump as Anthropic Debut Drains Liquidity
passages: Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year.

With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public.
As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically.

The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations.
Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention.
If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return.

What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge.

extraction.body: Bitcoin and ether just traced the same sharp sell-off pattern that preceded SpaceX's blockbuster IPO earlier this year, raising urgent questions about whether institutional money is abandoning crypto for hot tech listings. With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public. The crypto market just delivered an eerie sense of déjà vu. Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year. The correlation is raising uncomfortable questions for crypto bulls about whether institutional money views digital assets as a liquidity source to fund allocations in hot tech IPOs. As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically. The pattern matches what happened in the lead-up to SpaceX's listing, when both cryptocurrencies shed double-digit percentages before finding support only after the IPO priced. When a massive IPO looms, institutional investors appear to be liquidating portions of their crypto holdings to free up capital for new allocations. It's a liquidity rotation that hits hardest in the two to three weeks before pricing, precisely when underwriters are locking in final commitments from large buyers. Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention. But here's where it gets interesting for crypto traders. After SpaceX priced its IPO, bitcoin and ether both stabilized within days and then mounted modest recoveries over the following weeks. The theory goes that once institutional allocations are locked and IPO euphoria fades, some of that capital rotates back into crypto as investors rebalance portfolios. With Anthropic's first trading day in the books and the initial pop already priced in, crypto markets are testing whether they can find a floor. Bitcoin has shown some signs of stabilization, though trading volumes remain thin, suggesting many institutional players are still on the sidelines. What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge. That's a far cry from the narrative of bitcoin as digital gold or a portfolio hedge that trades independently of traditional markets. The institutional demand picture is murkier than it was during previous crypto rallies. While bitcoin ETFs have attracted steady inflows this year, the pace has slowed considerably. Meanwhile, the pipeline of major tech IPOs remains robust, with several AI and enterprise software unicorns reportedly preparing listings for early 2027. If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return. The key variable is whether another blockbuster IPO gets announced soon, which could trigger a repeat of the cycle. Some crypto analysts argue the sell-off is actually healthy, shaking out weak hands and establishing clearer support levels. Others worry it exposes how dependent crypto markets have become on the same institutional money that chases every hot tech trend. The difference in perspective often comes down to whether you view crypto as a mature asset class or still an emerging one fighting for legitimacy. Bitcoin is hovering near technical support levels that held during previous corrections, while ether faces a more uncertain picture given its underperformance. Trading desks report that institutional inquiry has picked up slightly since Anthropic's debut, but no one is ready to call a bottom yet. The broader implication is that crypto's fate may be more intertwined with the tech IPO calendar than many investors realized. As long as venture-backed unicorns keep going public at premium valuations, institutional investors may continue using crypto as a source of liquidity to fund those allocations. That's not necessarily bearish long-term, but it does suggest crypto markets could face periodic pressure whenever the IPO window heats up. The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations. Whether bitcoin and ether can establish a floor now that Anthropic's debut is complete will signal if the SpaceX playbook repeats, with capital gradually rotating back into digital assets. But with more AI unicorns eyeing 2027 listings, crypto investors may need to accept that their markets are now tethered to the tech IPO calendar in ways that challenge the independence narrative. The next few weeks will show if institutional demand returns or if crypto faces another cycle of liquidation as the next blockbuster listing approaches.

sources.title: Race to be next UN secretary general exposes divisions among world powers - The Guardian
passages: The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers.

The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council.
To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes.
The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres , but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance.

extraction.body: Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations . Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica , has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate. Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination. The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white. One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.” The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres , but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance. Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh , is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen. A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills. Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month. In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”. Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”. Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle. But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval. It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible. Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE. The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority. In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point. In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer. Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution. Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.

extraction.body: The headquarters of the United Nations in New York City. /VCG The UN Security Council on Friday held its ninth straw poll on candidates for the next UN secretary-general, Latvia's UN Ambassador Sanita Pavluta-Deslandes announced. Pavluta-Deslandes, whose country holds the council's rotating presidency for November, said the results would be conveyed to each candidate through the permanent representatives of the member states that nominated them. The president of the UN General Assembly would also be informed that the straw poll had been conducted, she told reporters. The Security Council uses straw polls, or informal closed-door ballots, to assess the viability of candidates. Their results are not officially released. Through the polling process, the Council determines which candidate to recommend to the General Assembly for appointment as the next secretary-general. Council members are believed to receive one ballot for each candidate, with three options: "encouraged," "discouraged" and "no opinion expressed." To secure the Council's recommendation, a candidate needs to receive at least nine "encouraged" votes and no "discouraged" votes from any of the five permanent members (P5) – Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States. As in the sixth straw poll held on October 16, Friday's ballots were color-coded to distinguish the voting intentions of the P5. According to leaked results, Rebeca Grynspan, a former vice president of Costa Rica and current secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, continued to lead in the race. Grynspan was followed by Rafael Grossi of Argentina, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency. The term of current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expires on December 31, 2026. His successor is expected to take office on January 1, 2027.

Costa Rican economist Rebeca Grynspan maintained her lead in the race to become the next United Nations secretary-general in Friday’s ninth Security Council straw poll, but the first color-coded ballot since October showed that she and the other leading candidates continue to face opposition from veto-wielding permanent members. Unlike the previous two rounds, which used undifferentiated ballots, Friday’s color-coded poll distinguished votes cast by the council’s five permanent members — the U.S., U.K., France, Russia and China — from those of its 10 elected members. While earlier polls showed several candidates emerging as front-runners, they obscured whether those contenders faced opposition from countries capable of blocking a formal recommendation. The last color-coded ballot, held Oct. 16, showed that no candidate had avoided discouragement votes from permanent members, a pattern that continued Friday. The vote came one day after President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held an unprecedented trilateral summit on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen, China. While the three leaders issued a joint declaration agreeing broadly on the need for U.N. reform, Friday’s fractured straw poll underscored that Washington, Beijing and Moscow don’t agree on who should lead the institution. The results, however, appeared to reinforce Grynspan’s position as the clear front-runner in the race. To secure the Security Council’s formal recommendation, a candidate must receive at least nine votes and avoid a negative vote from any of the five permanent members. Grynspan has led eight of the nine straw polls held since August and is the only contender to have reached the nine-vote threshold in every poll since September. Grynspan was also the only candidate to clear nine encouragement votes on Friday, finishing two votes ahead of her nearest rival with 10 encouragement votes, four discouragement votes and one “no opinion” vote — down from 12 encouragement votes and three discouragement votes in the eighth round on Nov. 5. Additionally, she was the only contender to receive encouragement votes from a majority of both council blocs, earning support from three of the five permanent members and seven of the 10 elected members. Still, two of Grynspan’s discouragement votes came from permanent members, leaving her with the challenge of overcoming opposition from two countries with veto power. Her candidacy has drawn criticism from pro-Israel groups over her tenure leading the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development, which under her leadership has issued reports sharply critical of the impact of Israeli policies on the Palestinian economy. Meanwhile, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi finished second overall with eight encouragement votes and six discouragement votes, including three discouragement votes from permanent members — a decline from the nine encouragement votes he received in both the seventh and eighth rounds. Lana Nusseibeh, the United Arab Emirates’ former ambassador to the U.N., received seven encouragement votes, six discouragement votes and two “no opinion” votes, matching her tally from the previous two rounds. Her late entry into the race on Oct. 21 fueled diplomatic speculation that major powers might coalesce around her as a consensus pick. But in her first color-coded poll since entering the contest, three of the five permanent members discouraged her candidacy, while two encouraged her, indicating that she faces resistance from the P5 as well as a more limited base of support among elected members. Nusseibeh’s bid has also faced scrutiny over allegations that the UAE has supplied the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group in Sudan’s civil war, a charge Abu Dhabi denies. Nusseibeh has condemned atrocities committed by the RSF and pledged to serve independently of the Emirati government if selected. Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, who had ranked among the top three contenders in earlier rounds, saw her support slip to six encouragement votes and six discouragement votes, including two from permanent members — down from eight encouragement votes in the previous round. Rodrigues Birkett has faced scrutiny over her strongly critical positions on Israel. Feridun Sinirlioğlu, Turkey’s newly nominated candidate, received five encouragement votes and 10 discouragement votes, four of which came from permanent members. Ankara entered Sinirlioğlu, a former foreign minister and U.N. ambassador, into the race on Nov. 1 after the selection process had stalled. But he has struggled to gain traction in his first two straw polls, having debuted with just three encouragement votes in the Nov. 5 round, and faces stiff opposition from permanent members. Speaking to reporters on Friday following leaked reports of the straw poll, Mike Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the U.N. said Washington would “welcome and encourage a candidate from Latin America to emerge,” showing support for the council’s informal regional rotation, which this year has included a push for a secretary general from Latin America and the Caribbean. “There is this informal rotation to the Western hemisphere. Of course, that’s the ‘United States’ hemisphere,’” Waltz said. “We also want the best candidate to emerge. Unfortunately, there hasn’t been consensus yet.” Waltz called on candidates that are “receiving very little encouragement” to “step aside.” “We certainly appreciate those who have stepped forward, put their vision forward, sought the support of the council and the broader membership here. But if they haven’t received it, we think it’s probably time to step aside and let the council consider a narrower field for those who are receiving some level of support,” he continued. The latest straw poll comes as the Security Council faces mounting pressure to recommend a successor before Secretary-General António Guterres’ second five-year term expires on Dec. 31. With no consensus yet among the five permanent members, the U.N. confronts the unprecedented prospect of entering 2027 without an appointed leader. Reuters reported Thursday that U.N. officials are drafting contingency plans in case no successor is selected by year’s end. Because the U.N. Charter does not specify how to handle a leadership vacuum, potential stopgaps include briefly extending Guterres’ term or naming one of his deputies to serve in an acting capacity. A former U.N. official told Reuters that while the Security Council and General Assembly could continue meeting without a secretary-general, key administrative functions — including senior appointments and budget decisions — would be disrupted.
