extraction.body: Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner Debate about dominance of permanent five members could reignite if major powers block Costa Rican frontrunner The race to become the next UN secretary general could reach a decisive moment on Friday when a UN security council vote is likely to reveal whether the Costa Rican frontrunner for the post would be blocked by the big powers. If so, the setback will reignite a debate about the dominance of the permanent five (P5) members at the United Nations . Rebeca Grynspan, an economist and UN insider who is from a family of Polish-Jewish wartime refugees to Costa Rica , has been in the lead in all but one of the eight straw polls of the 15 UN security council members since the first secret ballot was held on 30 July. Each member goes down the list of candidates, casting an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” vote for each candidate. Despite countries not being required to reveal how they voted, it is thought Grynspan’s candidature has been resisted by Russia and the US, two of the five permanent security council members that can ultimately wield a veto against a candidate. Knowledge among the security council delegations of how countries are voting is down to private intelligence, leaks and a process of elimination. The intensive lobbying over the job has spread across the globe, but Friday is especially important since the poll is slated to differentiate the voting of the P5 from the 10 elected members (E10) of the security council. To be recommended as secretary general to the UN general assembly, a candidate needs nine votes and no vetoes. In Friday’s colour-coded secret ballot, the P5 will cast red ballots and the E10 white. One diplomat said: “The electoral system means it is important how many votes you win, but equally how many of certain votes you don’t lose.” The protracted 140-day deadlock confirms the polarisation that has hampered the incumbent secretary general, António Guterres , but also belies claims the role is now an irrelevance. Friday’s secret ballot may also reveal whether the United Arab Emirates’ campaign for its diplomat, Lana Nusseibeh , is about to blow up in its face due to the hostility to the UAE’s brand of active, commercially driven diplomacy, not just in Sudan, but also Somalia, Western Sahara, Libya and Yemen. A late entrant, in the two straw polls in which she has contested so far, Nusseibeh secured only seven “encourage” votes, six “discourage” and two “no opinions”. This is despite prestigious big-power backing and her acknowledged personal diplomatic skills. Nusseibeh has US and Russian backing. The French foreign ministry may have misgivings about the UAE, but Emmanuel Macron, the French president, travelled to the UAE in the midst of French riots to see the UAE president, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, and secure 100,000 metric tons of diesel a month. In the UK, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has kept his counsel, but he shares a Polish-Jewish refugee heritage with Grynspan and cannot be an admirer of the UAE’s human rights record or its evasion of EU sanctions on Russia. The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has UAE connections from his time as mayor of Manchester, and Nusseibeh is a fellow alumnus of the University of Cambridge. At the UN she worked closely with the UK in an informal group called “Friends of the Future of the UN”. Yet 68 British MPs, including the Labour chair of the international development select committee, Sarah Champion, last week signed a letter calling on Burnham to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”. Some of the opposition to her from elected security council members is not wholly political. Latin American countries believe an informal rotation system means it is their turn to lead the UN. As a result Panama and Colombia, currently on the security council, will oppose her. China has also been supportive of this rotation principle. But others deeply object to what they consider to be the UAE’s dollar diplomacy and preparedness to use its extraordinary wealth to exacerbate and exploit pre-existing divisions in a country to gain a commercial foothold. Somalia, for instance, has a seat on the Security Council, and its president, Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, this week went on TV to accuse the UAE of buying ports, establishing military bases and supporting armed forces outside Somalia’s national security framework without federal approval. It is also possible that Finland and Latvia, the two elected members with the greatest stake in Ukraine, are unimpressed that the UAE gave Vladimir Putin red carpet treatment when he visited Abu Dhabi in December 2023, nine months after the international criminal court had issued an arrest warrant for child trafficking. Greece, less engaged in Ukraine, may be more flexible. Since the last poll, Nusseibeh has been to Bahrain, Britain and Pakistan, a clue as to where extra votes may be harvested. She also had a “thoughtful exchange” with Zeng Jixin, the Chinese ambassador to the UAE. The two hurdles are whether someone so deep inside the UAE inner circle would have the courage in office to show true independence, and whether her active denials of UAE involvement in arming the RSF in Sudan leave her irretrievably tainted. From a Palestinian intellectual family, she insists she would make peace in Sudan her number one priority. In the last ballot on 5 November, Grynspan won 12 votes in favour and three negative. But on 16 October – the only colour-coded ballot so far – which distinguishes between permanent and elected members – she received two discourage votes from permanent members, the equivalent of a veto. Nusseibeh had not joined the race at that point. In an administration as personalised as the US, it has been hard for Grynspan to gain influence, with many sensing that Mike Waltz, the US ambassador to the UN, is the key influencer. Grynspan has been reluctant to make the fact she is Jewish a feature of her candidacy, but the election of a Jewish person to run the UN might be seen as something the US could embrace as transformative. Her age – she is 70 – could be considered a drawback among those calling for a younger generation to renew the institution. Although there are other Latin American candidates, Grynspan is seen as a more viable candidate than her rival, the Argentine Rafael Grossi, the head of the UN weapons inspectorate. Russia has opposed Grossi, objecting to his interventions over the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant in Ukraine.

extraction.body: The headquarters of the United Nations in New York City. /VCG The UN Security Council on Friday held its ninth straw poll on candidates for the next UN secretary-general, Latvia's UN Ambassador Sanita Pavluta-Deslandes announced. Pavluta-Deslandes, whose country holds the council's rotating presidency for November, said the results would be conveyed to each candidate through the permanent representatives of the member states that nominated them. The president of the UN General Assembly would also be informed that the straw poll had been conducted, she told reporters. The Security Council uses straw polls, or informal closed-door ballots, to assess the viability of candidates. Their results are not officially released. Through the polling process, the Council determines which candidate to recommend to the General Assembly for appointment as the next secretary-general. Council members are believed to receive one ballot for each candidate, with three options: "encouraged," "discouraged" and "no opinion expressed." To secure the Council's recommendation, a candidate needs to receive at least nine "encouraged" votes and no "discouraged" votes from any of the five permanent members (P5) – Britain, China, France, Russia and the United States. As in the sixth straw poll held on October 16, Friday's ballots were color-coded to distinguish the voting intentions of the P5. According to leaked results, Rebeca Grynspan, a former vice president of Costa Rica and current secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, continued to lead in the race. Grynspan was followed by Rafael Grossi of Argentina, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency. The term of current UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expires on December 31, 2026. His successor is expected to take office on January 1, 2027.

Costa Rican economist Rebeca Grynspan maintained her lead in the race to become the next United Nations secretary-general in Friday’s ninth Security Council straw poll, but the first color-coded ballot since October showed that she and the other leading candidates continue to face opposition from veto-wielding permanent members. Unlike the previous two rounds, which used undifferentiated ballots, Friday’s color-coded poll distinguished votes cast by the council’s five permanent members — the U.S., U.K., France, Russia and China — from those of its 10 elected members. While earlier polls showed several candidates emerging as front-runners, they obscured whether those contenders faced opposition from countries capable of blocking a formal recommendation. The last color-coded ballot, held Oct. 16, showed that no candidate had avoided discouragement votes from permanent members, a pattern that continued Friday. The vote came one day after President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin held an unprecedented trilateral summit on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation gathering in Shenzhen, China. While the three leaders issued a joint declaration agreeing broadly on the need for U.N. reform, Friday’s fractured straw poll underscored that Washington, Beijing and Moscow don’t agree on who should lead the institution. The results, however, appeared to reinforce Grynspan’s position as the clear front-runner in the race. To secure the Security Council’s formal recommendation, a candidate must receive at least nine votes and avoid a negative vote from any of the five permanent members. Grynspan has led eight of the nine straw polls held since August and is the only contender to have reached the nine-vote threshold in every poll since September. Grynspan was also the only candidate to clear nine encouragement votes on Friday, finishing two votes ahead of her nearest rival with 10 encouragement votes, four discouragement votes and one “no opinion” vote — down from 12 encouragement votes and three discouragement votes in the eighth round on Nov. 5. Additionally, she was the only contender to receive encouragement votes from a majority of both council blocs, earning support from three of the five permanent members and seven of the 10 elected members. Still, two of Grynspan’s discouragement votes came from permanent members, leaving her with the challenge of overcoming opposition from two countries with veto power. Her candidacy has drawn criticism from pro-Israel groups over her tenure leading the U.N. Conference on Trade and Development, which under her leadership has issued reports sharply critical of the impact of Israeli policies on the Palestinian economy. Meanwhile, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi finished second overall with eight encouragement votes and six discouragement votes, including three discouragement votes from permanent members — a decline from the nine encouragement votes he received in both the seventh and eighth rounds. Lana Nusseibeh, the United Arab Emirates’ former ambassador to the U.N., received seven encouragement votes, six discouragement votes and two “no opinion” votes, matching her tally from the previous two rounds. Her late entry into the race on Oct. 21 fueled diplomatic speculation that major powers might coalesce around her as a consensus pick. But in her first color-coded poll since entering the contest, three of the five permanent members discouraged her candidacy, while two encouraged her, indicating that she faces resistance from the P5 as well as a more limited base of support among elected members. Nusseibeh’s bid has also faced scrutiny over allegations that the UAE has supplied the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group in Sudan’s civil war, a charge Abu Dhabi denies. Nusseibeh has condemned atrocities committed by the RSF and pledged to serve independently of the Emirati government if selected. Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, who had ranked among the top three contenders in earlier rounds, saw her support slip to six encouragement votes and six discouragement votes, including two from permanent members — down from eight encouragement votes in the previous round. Rodrigues Birkett has faced scrutiny over her strongly critical positions on Israel. Feridun Sinirlioğlu, Turkey’s newly nominated candidate, received five encouragement votes and 10 discouragement votes, four of which came from permanent members. Ankara entered Sinirlioğlu, a former foreign minister and U.N. ambassador, into the race on Nov. 1 after the selection process had stalled. But he has struggled to gain traction in his first two straw polls, having debuted with just three encouragement votes in the Nov. 5 round, and faces stiff opposition from permanent members. Speaking to reporters on Friday following leaked reports of the straw poll, Mike Waltz, U.S. ambassador to the U.N. said Washington would “welcome and encourage a candidate from Latin America to emerge,” showing support for the council’s informal regional rotation, which this year has included a push for a secretary general from Latin America and the Caribbean. “There is this informal rotation to the Western hemisphere. Of course, that’s the ‘United States’ hemisphere,’” Waltz said. “We also want the best candidate to emerge. Unfortunately, there hasn’t been consensus yet.” Waltz called on candidates that are “receiving very little encouragement” to “step aside.” “We certainly appreciate those who have stepped forward, put their vision forward, sought the support of the council and the broader membership here. But if they haven’t received it, we think it’s probably time to step aside and let the council consider a narrower field for those who are receiving some level of support,” he continued. The latest straw poll comes as the Security Council faces mounting pressure to recommend a successor before Secretary-General António Guterres’ second five-year term expires on Dec. 31. With no consensus yet among the five permanent members, the U.N. confronts the unprecedented prospect of entering 2027 without an appointed leader. Reuters reported Thursday that U.N. officials are drafting contingency plans in case no successor is selected by year’s end. Because the U.N. Charter does not specify how to handle a leadership vacuum, potential stopgaps include briefly extending Guterres’ term or naming one of his deputies to serve in an acting capacity. A former U.N. official told Reuters that while the Security Council and General Assembly could continue meeting without a secretary-general, key administrative functions — including senior appointments and budget decisions — would be disrupted. TAIPEI – Tech executive Alice Huang is the woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Jensen Huang, head of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia, according to media reports. Public details are sparse about the woman, also known as Huang Le, who had reportedly been a top figure at a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed International. Here is what we know about her and the company. Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen recruited by Beijing to collect intelligence on the Nvidia boss, according to The New York Times, which first reported that Jensen Huang was the alleged target of a spy plot. Despite their shared surname, Alice Huang is no relation to the 63-year-old Taiwan-born head of the world’s most valuable company. The Times, citing people briefed on the surveillance, said that Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected at the highest level of the global AI chip industry. The sector is highly sensitive as the United States and China race to develop advanced AI systems with potential military applications. An online search brought up a short profile for Alice Huang, with her photo, on a Chinese fund database. It listed previous jobs including at HSBC bank, and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV. AFP was unable to verify the contents of the profile or who had written it, but has attempted to contact the companies cited. Media reports last week said they had a close relationship, and Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees on Nov 8 that he was “deeply sorry” for being “unfaithful to my wife”. One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show the leather jacket-clad Nvidia boss sitting next to a long-haired woman in glitzy jewellery believed to be Alice Huang. The following year, they both attended a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a Chinese restaurant in Taiwan during Computex, the island’s top tech expo. Journalists stood outside the restaurant filming through glass windows and doors as Jensen Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, who was wearing a pink dress, mingled with other attendees. At one point, Jensen Huang can be seen putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the right cheek, press live streams show. Alice Huang is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after talking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back. They later leave the restaurant in the same car. US officials concluded in 2025 that Alice Huang was targeting Jensen Huang as a spy, according to The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal. At the time, Alice Huang was said to be a top executive at data centre firm Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power to other companies to train and run AI. Megaspeed’s website says it is “a core business partner of Nvidia’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region”. On LinkedIn, it says it has offices in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, with around two to 10 employees and 25 “associated members”. When AFP called the number listed on Megaspeed’s website, the person who answered said they were unfamiliar with the company and that the number was a residential line. The firm was previously called 7Road International, according to the Singapore Government’s website, suggesting links to Chinese gaming company 7Road. Washington restricts the export to China of Nvidia’s most cutting-edge silicon chips, citing national security concerns but also seen as a measure to stay ahead in AI. The New York Times said the US government had been probing Megaspeed since 2024 over its potential steering of Nvidia chips to China. The company has also reportedly been under investigation by the Singapore authorities, who The Times says questioned Alice Huang in 2025. AFP has contacted Singapore’s police and the Home Affairs Ministry for comment. In 2025, Bloomberg News also reported on the Singaporean probe into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China. In December 2025, Megaspeed said Bloomberg’s reporting “contains misleading information and incorrect insinuations, including suggestions that we may have been involved in illegal chip transfers”. AFP

sources.title: Nvidia scandal: Alice Huang's family linked to Chinese military suppliers, NYT reports
passages: Companies linked to Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman at the center of the Nvidia espionage scandal, have extensive connections to China's defense industry through her family members and business associates, according to a New York Times investigation published Friday.

The findings add another dimension to the controversy surrounding Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, who had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of working for Beijing's intelligence services.

The investigation found that approximately $3.6 billion in Chinese government funding flowed through companies associated with Huang's relatives or business partners, financing technology projects that included data centers equipped with Nvidia chips.

Senior U.S. national security officials have long expressed concern that China could obtain advanced Nvidia processors, technology that could help Beijing develop sophisticated military systems powered by artificial intelligence.

On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee took the unusual step of releasing confidential information concerning applications submitted by Nvidia for licenses to legally export its advanced H200 artificial intelligence chips to Chinese customers.

An analysis by Strider Technologies and a review of corporate records identified a network involving Alice Huang, her sister Huang Yu and an investor named Kang Wei, who was Huang's business partner and was frequently presented as her husband.

The investigation raises broader concerns about the complex corporate structures through which advanced American technology can become accessible to Chinese entities, including companies with links to Beijing's military-industrial sector.
Other companies in the network lease servers powered by Nvidia chips through arrangements financed by a business affiliated with China's largest military aircraft manufacturer.

Justice Department is investigating one of those companies over suspected smuggling of advanced semiconductor chips into China. 'Follow the money, and you find China's military' U.S. officials are continuing to examine Huang's activities and her alleged efforts to facilitate the supply of advanced chips to China.
The spokesperson emphasized that Nvidia had never supplied H200 chips to the Century Litong subsidiary in question and would not do so in the future.

extraction.body: Companies linked to Alice Huang, the Chinese businesswoman at the center of the Nvidia espionage scandal, have extensive connections to China's defense industry through her family members and business associates, according to a New York Times investigation published Friday. The findings reveal a network of direct and indirect ties connecting companies that purchased Nvidia chips to state-owned Chinese defense contractors supplying equipment to the country's military. The investigation found that approximately $3.6 billion in Chinese government funding flowed through companies associated with Huang's relatives or business partners, financing technology projects that included data centers equipped with Nvidia chips. However, the precise nature of Huang's relationship with China's defense industry remains unclear. Crucially, investigators have not established whether Nvidia chips ultimately ended up being used in Chinese military projects. The findings add another dimension to the controversy surrounding Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang, who had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese national whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of working for Beijing's intelligence services. Senior U.S. national security officials have long expressed concern that China could obtain advanced Nvidia processors, technology that could help Beijing develop sophisticated military systems powered by artificial intelligence. $3.6 billion in Chinese government funding The New York Times investigation cites a confidential report prepared by Strider Technologies, an independent intelligence firm specializing in corporate intelligence and employing former intelligence officers and China experts. The report found that approximately $3.6 billion in Chinese government funds passed through businesses linked to Huang's relatives and associates. The money supported technology projects, including data centers that received Nvidia processors, according to the investigation. Last month, the New York Times reported that U.S. officials believed Huang, also known as Huang Le, had served as a Chinese intelligence source and provided information to China's Ministry of State Security, the country's principal civilian intelligence agency. An analysis by Strider Technologies and a review of corporate records identified a network involving Alice Huang, her sister Huang Yu and an investor named Kang Wei, who was Huang's business partner and was frequently presented as her husband. The companies connect authorized Nvidia partners capable of purchasing advanced artificial intelligence chips with technology projects linked to the Chinese government and military. According to the New York Times, companies within Huang's family network jointly own a cybersecurity venture with an arm of China Electronics Technology Group, a major state-owned defense electronics conglomerate. Other companies in the network lease servers powered by Nvidia chips through arrangements financed by a business affiliated with China's largest military aircraft manufacturer. In another case, a company in the network and a manufacturer of radar and missile components share the same parent company. The investigation also found that two authorized Nvidia partners have connections to Huang. Justice Department is investigating one of those companies over suspected smuggling of advanced semiconductor chips into China. 'Follow the money, and you find China's military' U.S. officials are continuing to examine Huang's activities and her alleged efforts to facilitate the supply of advanced chips to China. According to people briefed on the American investigation, one of the central questions is the extent of Huang's relationships with China's military and companies under its control. Greg Levesque, CEO of Strider Technologies, told the New York Times that Beijing had spent years developing networks reaching deep into Western economies. "When you follow the money, far too often you find the Chinese military at the end of the trail," he said. Levesque argued that China increasingly relies on Western technology, capital and professional expertise to develop the industrial infrastructure supporting its defense establishment. The investigation raises broader concerns about the complex corporate structures through which advanced American technology can become accessible to Chinese entities, including companies with links to Beijing's military-industrial sector. Nvidia sought licenses for more than 40,000 chips The revelations come as U.S. lawmakers intensify their scrutiny of Nvidia's business dealings with Chinese companies. On Thursday, the House Foreign Affairs Committee took the unusual step of releasing confidential information concerning applications submitted by Nvidia for licenses to legally export its advanced H200 artificial intelligence chips to Chinese customers. The newly disclosed records show that Nvidia sought permission to sell more than 40,000 H200 chips to a subsidiary of Century Litong, a Chinese company connected to Alice Huang. The disclosure raised new questions about the potential recipients of some of Nvidia's most sophisticated processors and the ability of U.S. export controls to prevent sensitive technology from reaching companies connected to China's defense industry. An Nvidia spokesperson said that although the company had received some export licenses, it had already stopped shipping H200 chips to China. The spokesperson emphasized that Nvidia had never supplied H200 chips to the Century Litong subsidiary in question and would not do so in the future. The distinction remains central to the investigation: Corporate relationships and export applications demonstrate the existence of commercial links, but they do not establish that Nvidia processors were ultimately delivered to, or used by, China's military. For U.S. investigators, the unresolved question is whether the network surrounding Huang merely connected Chinese technology businesses to government-backed projects or also provided a pathway through which advanced American AI capabilities could support Beijing's military ambitions.

[NEW YORK] Alibaba was sued on Thursday (Nov 20) in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang contributed to his resignation on Nov 11.

According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business.

Shareholders cited Alibaba’s relationship with Megaspeed, a ​Singapore company suspected of helping Beijing gain access to advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence chips, and whose executive Alice Huang had a relationship with Jensen Huang, who is not related to her.

The shareholders said Alibaba shares fell 14 per cent over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba’s ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed’s “dominant” customer.

They attributed part of the decline to a Nov 12 Reuters article that said Nvidia’s spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies’ remote use of ‌advanced processors.
Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Eddie Wu, its chief executive, is also a defendant.
Sustainability has reached APAC boardrooms but are board members sufficiently equipped? Find out more in our report.
Nvidia itself faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors.

Wu said on Thursday that Alibaba remained on track for US$100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20 per cent earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation margin by 2030, despite US curbs on access to computing power that could affect the company’s products and services next year.
The restrictions were imposed after Huang resigned from Nvidia.
In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of “Chinese military companies” that the Department of Defense linked to that country’s military.

In October, a federal judge in California granted Alibaba an injunction barring the US government from denying Pentagon ​contracts to companies with lobbyists also working with designated Chinese military companies.
Alibaba said that restriction caused its lobbyists to retreat because they feared losing other clients, and violated its First Amendment constitutional right to speak to and petition the government.
Thursday’s lawsuit by Alibaba shareholder Withida Bihan seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba’s American depositary shares between May 23, 2024 and Nov 11, 2026. REUTERS

TAIPEI – Tech executive Alice Huang is the woman accused of spying for China during an affair with Jensen Huang, head of US artificial intelligence chip titan Nvidia, according to media reports. Public details are sparse about the woman, also known as Huang Le, who had reportedly been a top figure at a Singapore-based data centre company called Megaspeed International. Here is what we know about her and the company. Alice Huang is a Chinese citizen recruited by Beijing to collect intelligence on the Nvidia boss, according to The New York Times, which first reported that Jensen Huang was the alleged target of a spy plot. Despite their shared surname, Alice Huang is no relation to the 63-year-old Taiwan-born head of the world’s most valuable company. The Times, citing people briefed on the surveillance, said that Alice Huang speaks good English and is well connected at the highest level of the global AI chip industry. The sector is highly sensitive as the United States and China race to develop advanced AI systems with potential military applications. An online search brought up a short profile for Alice Huang, with her photo, on a Chinese fund database. It listed previous jobs including at HSBC bank, and as a reporter for Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV. AFP was unable to verify the contents of the profile or who had written it, but has attempted to contact the companies cited. Media reports last week said they had a close relationship, and Jensen Huang told Nvidia employees on Nov 8 that he was “deeply sorry” for being “unfaithful to my wife”. One photo from an industry party in 2024, posted on LinkedIn, appears to show the leather jacket-clad Nvidia boss sitting next to a long-haired woman in glitzy jewellery believed to be Alice Huang. The following year, they both attended a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang at a Chinese restaurant in Taiwan during Computex, the island’s top tech expo. Journalists stood outside the restaurant filming through glass windows and doors as Jensen Huang and a woman identified as Alice Huang, who was wearing a pink dress, mingled with other attendees. At one point, Jensen Huang can be seen putting his arm around Alice Huang as she kisses him on the right cheek, press live streams show. Alice Huang is also seen following the Nvidia chief as he re-enters the restaurant after talking to journalists outside, running her fingers down his lower back. They later leave the restaurant in the same car. US officials concluded in 2025 that Alice Huang was targeting Jensen Huang as a spy, according to The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal. At the time, Alice Huang was said to be a top executive at data centre firm Megaspeed International, which rents out computing power to other companies to train and run AI. Megaspeed’s website says it is “a core business partner of Nvidia’s computing power cloud business in the Asia-Pacific region”. On LinkedIn, it says it has offices in Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia, with around two to 10 employees and 25 “associated members”. When AFP called the number listed on Megaspeed’s website, the person who answered said they were unfamiliar with the company and that the number was a residential line. The firm was previously called 7Road International, according to the Singapore Government’s website, suggesting links to Chinese gaming company 7Road. Washington restricts the export to China of Nvidia’s most cutting-edge silicon chips, citing national security concerns but also seen as a measure to stay ahead in AI. The New York Times said the US government had been probing Megaspeed since 2024 over its potential steering of Nvidia chips to China. The company has also reportedly been under investigation by the Singapore authorities, who The Times says questioned Alice Huang in 2025. AFP has contacted Singapore’s police and the Home Affairs Ministry for comment. In 2025, Bloomberg News also reported on the Singaporean probe into Megaspeed over the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China. In December 2025, Megaspeed said Bloomberg’s reporting “contains misleading information and incorrect insinuations, including suggestions that we may have been involved in illegal chip transfers”. sources.title: Shareholders sue Alibaba for allegedly hiding ties to Alice Huang, the suspected spy in Nvidia scandal - The Business Times
passages: [NEW YORK] Alibaba was sued on Thursday (Nov 20) in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang contributed to his resignation on Nov 11.

The shareholders said Alibaba shares fell 14 per cent over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba’s ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed’s “dominant” customer.

According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business.
Thursday’s lawsuit by Alibaba shareholder Withida Bihan seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba’s American depositary shares between May 23, 2024 and Nov 11, 2026.

They attributed part of the decline to a Nov 12 Reuters article that said Nvidia’s spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies’ remote use of ‌advanced processors.
Nvidia itself faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors.
The restrictions were imposed after Huang resigned from Nvidia.
In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of “Chinese military companies” that the Department of Defense linked to that country’s military.
Alibaba said that restriction caused its lobbyists to retreat because they feared losing other clients, and violated its First Amendment constitutional right to speak to and petition the government.
Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Eddie Wu, its chief executive, is also a defendant.
South-east Asia has lost Nvidia’s best salesman

[NEW YORK] Alibaba was sued on Thursday (Nov 20) in New York by shareholders who accused the Chinese e-commerce giant of defrauding them by concealing its ties to the suspected Chinese spy, whose relationship with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang contributed to his resignation on Nov 11.

According to a proposed class action filed in Manhattan federal court, Alibaba inflated its share price by knowingly and materially understating in its 2024, 2025 and 2026 annual reports the risks that actual or suspected export control violations could harm its business.

Shareholders cited Alibaba’s relationship with Megaspeed, a ​Singapore company suspected of helping Beijing gain access to advanced Nvidia artificial intelligence chips, and whose executive Alice Huang had a relationship with Jensen Huang, who is not related to her.

The shareholders said Alibaba shares fell 14 per cent over four days last week because of media reports on Alibaba’s ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed, including that Alibaba had become Megaspeed’s “dominant” customer.

They attributed part of the decline to a Nov 12 Reuters article that said Nvidia’s spy scandal could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on Chinese AI companies’ remote use of ‌advanced processors.
Alibaba did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Eddie Wu, its chief executive, is also a defendant.
Sustainability has reached APAC boardrooms but are board members sufficiently equipped? Find out more in our report.
Nvidia itself faces several shareholder lawsuits over the spy scandal, including allegations of lax oversight by its directors.

Wu said on Thursday that Alibaba remained on track for US$100 billion in external cloud revenue and a 20 per cent earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation margin by 2030, despite US curbs on access to computing power that could affect the company’s products and services next year.
The restrictions were imposed after Huang resigned from Nvidia.
In June, Alibaba sued the US government over being added to a blacklist of “Chinese military companies” that the Department of Defense linked to that country’s military.

In October, a federal judge in California granted Alibaba an injunction barring the US government from denying Pentagon ​contracts to companies with lobbyists also working with designated Chinese military companies.
Alibaba said that restriction caused its lobbyists to retreat because they feared losing other clients, and violated its First Amendment constitutional right to speak to and petition the government.
Thursday’s lawsuit by Alibaba shareholder Withida Bihan seeks unspecified damages for holders of Alibaba’s American depositary shares between May 23, 2024 and Nov 11, 2026. REUTERS

extraction.body: Bitcoin 's latest sell-off is reviving doubts that it can behave as the "digital gold" market hedge that crypto backers have long envisioned. Coming into 2026, experts said that showing bitcoin could serve as a market hedge rather than a risk-on asset that moves up and down with growth stocks was an important test for the cryptocurrency. Bitcoin was trading under $62,000 on Friday morning, down from an all-time high of more than $126,000 in early October last year. Its downward spiral in recent months and weeks has been precipitated by a confluence of factors. The heavy midterm elections losses for the Republicans, the Binance hack, and a world on edge about the security of all things technology — FAA ground stop, the outage of the National Security Agency's highly classified internal communications system, several online banking outages — have not helped the mood when it comes to putting trust in the digital world. But the market itself may be the biggest factor. Investors are currently in sell everything mode, including tech stocks and gold — the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 tumbled into correction territory on Friday, according to CNBC data. Bitcoin's recent price action has also tracked the move in the biggest tech IPOs , SpaceX and Anthropic. Taken together, the cryptocurrency is failing the test again when it comes to showing its worth as a market hedge during times of investor anxiety. In the past month alone, bitcoin had dropped roughly $20,000, as of Friday morning, according to CNBC data. Investors and financial management firms aren't viewing it as safe an investment as in the past, said Ryan Kirkley, co-founder and chief executive of Global Settlement Network, a Miami-based fintech that provides infrastructure for currency settlement, including crypto. "There's a bit more caution than there was a year ago." What is behind bitcoin's fall, and what is in store for its future? Here is what experts say. There have been many theories about how bitcoin would react based on different market and economic conditions. But historically, bitcoin has done best in low-rate environments and when lending opportunities are plentiful, said Juan Xavier Sanchez, head of wealth strategy at Activest Wealth Management in Aventura, Florida. When rates are down and treasuries aren't paying good yields, people tend to be more risk-seeking for higher returns. "Bitcoin for many investors is in that bucket," Sanchez said. Experts have noted that gold, which is now down over 35% from its early 2026 peak, is less attractive when cash accounts are paying 5%. Investments like gold and bitcoin offer no yield. Bitcoin's rising correlation with the Nasdaq-100 since late September suggests the two are increasingly moving in tandem, according to data from Fairlead Strategies, a technical research firm. That's consistent with an environment of higher volatility in which correlations across risk assets tend to increase. However, the correlation remains below its early-2026 highs, the data show. Bitcoin has certain characteristics of digital gold, in that it has a limited supply, no single owner and no CEO or board that can decide to issue more, said Anthony Georgiades, founder and general partner at Innovating Capital in New York, which invests in early-stage crypto, blockchain, digital infrastructure and deep tech companies. But it's also been caught up in monetary policy since its inception. The last decade or so of monetary policy has been extremely rewarding to speculative risk-on assets, Georgiades said. However, in periods of volatility, those types of assets have experienced the most significant drawdowns and have been the most heavily punished, Georgiades said. That means that a shock on one side of the board that might be completely independent of bitcoin could trigger a large volatility event "given how intertwined digital assets have become in the overall financial system," he said. Notably, bitcoin hasn't acted much like digital gold in more recent years, said Abe Sheikh, chief investment officer of Cordoba Advisory Partners in New York. In fact, it has fallen substantially during periods when the stock market has been falling. For example, from October 6 through November 18, the S&P 500 fell about 6.3%, and bitcoin fell around 27%. From January 21, 2025 through April 8, 2025, the S&P dropped around 17.4%, while bitcoin slid 27.8%, he said. Democrats gaining control over both houses is viewed as a negative for crypto from a market perspective. The crypto industry spent more than $200 million to support crypto-friendly candidates, but its role had less of an impact on overall results than in the last election cycle. However, bitcoin's downward trend was already in the works, said Cyrus Amini, chief investment officer at Hyphen Wealth Management in Lafayette, California. In September, the Clarity Act failed in the U.S. Senate, and while its outlook is now dim , according to many political and market experts, some form of crypto legislation is still considered a priority for many Democrats and Republicans, while the Trump-appointed heads of the Commodity Future Trading Commission and Securities and Exchange Commission continue to favor crypto in rulemaking. This fall, investors also started to question the security of encryption technology, leading to more concerns over the security of their bitcoin holdings, said Kirkley of Global Settlement Network. The Binance hack in October muddied the waters further. And the recent stock market jitters and economic concerns piled on doubts, Kirkley said. The last few weeks have been especially rough with data security concerns from multiple fronts, he added. Wall Street's embrace of bitcoin has been a big positive for the cryptocurrency. Kirkley noted that 20% of bitcoin's market price is coming from institutional investors, and that's a conservative estimate. In addition, new research from digital assets company Galaxy shows that a record 40.5% of all 13F-reported spot bitcoin exchange-traded product holdings, and 11.2% of all the bitcoin in the funds, came from advisory and wealth planning firms, such as RIAs and brokerage platforms, as of the third quarter 13F filings with the SEC, which are required of firms with over $100 million in assets to report their holdings. Much of this investment is through bitcoin spot ETFs like the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) that track its price. These ETFs, first approved by the SEC in January 2024, were supposed to provide a reliable new source of institutional demand. But ETF ownership also makes bitcoin especially easy to sell. Outflows from several of these funds have been substantial in recent months. IBIT, the largest of its peers, had six-month net outflows of $1.65 billion through Nov. 18 and one-month outflows of $1.37 billion, according to ETF Database. The second biggest, Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC ) had one-month net outflows of $322.65 million and six-month net outflows of $771.86 million, according to ETF Database. Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ( BTC ) had one-month net outflows of $66.35 million, though it had inflows of $590.04 million over six months. As of September 2026, public companies collectively hold close to 1.29 million bitcoins, which is more than 6% of the 21 million coins in existence, according to bitcoin.com . Most public companies invest their corporate treasury portfolios in low-risk, highly liquid instruments such as money market funds, Treasury bonds and Treasury bills. That said, there are some well-known companies that have invested in bitcoin. SpaceX, for example, purchased 18,712 bitcoins for a total cost of $661 million, at an average price of $35,324 per coin. The company began accumulating bitcoin in early 2021 and held its position unchanged from mid-2024 until its IPO filing . Digital Asset Treasury companies, known as DATs or DATCOs, have also played a role in bitcoin's volatility . DATs are publicly listed firms whose primary business strategy involves holding significant quantities of digital assets, such as bitcoin or ethereum , on their corporate balance sheets to drive shareholder value. Companies in this space include Strategy , Strive, and Twenty One Capital. "DATs have exacerbated the problem," said Sheikh of Cordoba Advisory Partners. When bitcoin is rising, these companies borrow money in the debt market or raise capital to buy more bitcoin, which magnifies the upswings. They have also sold bitcoin to make their bond coupon payments. "It leads to enormous volatility on the upside and downside," Sheikh said. As of mid-November, Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, holds 850,849 BTC, according to a regulatory filing . That represents roughly 4% of bitcoin's total supply. The company acquired these holdings at a total cost of approximately $64.2 billion, with an average purchase price of roughly $75,452 per coin, according to the filing. Bitcoin has been trending lower since the peak in October 2025. A trading range has taken hold and the bottom of the range is just below 60,000, said Katie Stockton, founder and managing partner of Fairlead Strategies. "It appears to be trying to find a footing," she said. Oversold conditions on the heels of recent lows in June and July, in addition to long-term momentum, suggest bitcoin can support an upturn, she said. But that depends on whether the crypto can hold at a current range around $60,000, she said. "At the end of the day, bitcoin is exceptionally volatile. Coming into 2026, experts said that showing bitcoin could serve as a market hedge rather than a risk-on asset that moves up and down with growth stocks was an important test for the cryptocurrency.

Bitcoin was trading under $62,000 on Friday morning, down from an all-time high of more than $126,000 in early October last year. Its downward spiral in recent months and weeks has been precipitated by a confluence of factors. The heavy midterm elections losses for the Republicans, the Binance hack, and a world on edge about the security of all things technology — FAA ground stop, the outage of the National Security Agency's highly classified internal communications system, several online banking outages — have not helped the mood when it comes to putting trust in the digital world.

But the market itself may be the biggest factor. Investors are currently in sell everything mode, including tech stocks and gold — the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 tumbled into correction territory on Friday, according to CNBC data. Bitcoin's recent price action has also tracked the move in the biggest tech IPOs , SpaceX and Anthropic. Taken together, the cryptocurrency is failing the test again when it comes to showing its worth as a market hedge during times of investor anxiety.
In the past month alone, bitcoin had dropped roughly $20,000, as of Friday morning, according to CNBC data.

Investors and financial management firms aren't viewing it as safe an investment as in the past, said Ryan Kirkley, co-founder and chief executive of Global Settlement Network, a Miami-based fintech that provides infrastructure for currency settlement, including crypto. "There's a bit more caution than there was a year ago."
What is behind bitcoin's fall, and what is in store for its future? Here is what experts say.

There have been many theories about how bitcoin would react based on different market and economic conditions. But historically, bitcoin has done best in low-rate environments and when lending opportunities are plentiful, said Juan Xavier Sanchez, head of wealth strategy at Activest Wealth Management in Aventura, Florida.
When rates are down and treasuries aren't paying good yields, people tend to be more risk-seeking for higher returns. "Bitcoin for many investors is in that bucket," Sanchez said.
Experts have noted that gold, which is now down over 35% from its early 2026 peak, is less attractive when cash accounts are paying 5%. Investments like gold and bitcoin offer no yield.

Bitcoin's rising correlation with the Nasdaq-100 since late September suggests the two are increasingly moving in tandem, according to data from Fairlead Strategies, a technical research firm. That's consistent with an environment of higher volatility in which correlations across risk assets tend to increase. However, the correlation remains below its early-2026 highs, the data show.

Bitcoin has certain characteristics of digital gold, in that it has a limited supply, no single owner and no CEO or board that can decide to issue more, said Anthony Georgiades, founder and general partner at Innovating Capital in New York, which invests in early-stage crypto, blockchain, digital infrastructure and deep tech companies.

But it's also been caught up in monetary policy since its inception. The last decade or so of monetary policy has been extremely rewarding to speculative risk-on assets, Georgiades said. However, in periods of volatility, those types of assets have experienced the most significant drawdowns and have been the most heavily punished, Georgiades said. That means that a shock on one side of the board that might be completely independent of bitcoin could trigger a large volatility event "given how intertwined digital assets have become in the overall financial system," he said.

Notably, bitcoin hasn't acted much like digital gold in more recent years, said Abe Sheikh, chief investment officer of Cordoba Advisory Partners in New York. In fact, it has fallen substantially during periods when the stock market has been falling. For example, from October 6 through November 18, the S&P 500 fell about 6.3%, and bitcoin fell around 27%. From January 21, 2025 through April 8, 2025, the S&P dropped around 17.4%, while bitcoin slid 27.8%, he said.

Democrats gaining control over both houses is viewed as a negative for crypto from a market perspective. The crypto industry spent more than $200 million to support crypto-friendly candidates, but its role had less of an impact on overall results than in the last election cycle. However, bitcoin's downward trend was already in the works, said Cyrus Amini, chief investment officer at Hyphen Wealth Management in Lafayette, California.

In September, the Clarity Act failed in the U.S. Senate, and while its outlook is now dim , according to many political and market experts, some form of crypto legislation is still considered a priority for many Democrats and Republicans, while the Trump-appointed heads of the Commodity Future Trading Commission and Securities and Exchange Commission continue to favor crypto in rulemaking.

This fall, investors also started to question the security of encryption technology, leading to more concerns over the security of their bitcoin holdings, said Kirkley of Global Settlement Network. The Binance hack in October muddied the waters further. And the recent stock market jitters and economic concerns piled on doubts, Kirkley said. The last few weeks have been especially rough with data security concerns from multiple fronts, he added.

Wall Street's embrace of bitcoin has been a big positive for the cryptocurrency. Kirkley noted that 20% of bitcoin's market price is coming from institutional investors, and that's a conservative estimate.

In addition, new research from digital assets company Galaxy shows that a record 40.5% of all 13F-reported spot bitcoin exchange-traded product holdings, and 11.2% of all the bitcoin in the funds, came from advisory and wealth planning firms, such as RIAs and brokerage platforms, as of the third quarter 13F filings with the SEC, which are required of firms with over $100 million in assets to report their holdings.

Much of this investment is through bitcoin spot ETFs like the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) that track its price. These ETFs, first approved by the SEC in January 2024, were supposed to provide a reliable new source of institutional demand. But ETF ownership also makes bitcoin especially easy to sell.

Outflows from several of these funds have been substantial in recent months. IBIT, the largest of its peers, had six-month net outflows of $1.65 billion through Nov. 18 and one-month outflows of $1.37 billion, according to ETF Database. The second biggest, Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC ) had one-month net outflows of $322.65 million and six-month net outflows of $771.86 million, according to ETF Database. Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ( BTC ) had one-month net outflows of $66.35 million, though it had inflows of $590.04 million over six months.
As of September 2026, public companies collectively hold close to 1.29 million bitcoins, which is more than 6% of the 21 million coins in existence, according to bitcoin.com .

Most public companies invest their corporate treasury portfolios in low-risk, highly liquid instruments such as money market funds, Treasury bonds and Treasury bills. That said, there are some well-known companies that have invested in bitcoin. SpaceX, for example, purchased 18,712 bitcoins for a total cost of $661 million, at an average price of $35,324 per coin. The company began accumulating bitcoin in early 2021 and held its position unchanged from mid-2024 until its IPO filing .

Digital Asset Treasury companies, known as DATs or DATCOs, have also played a role in bitcoin's volatility . DATs are publicly listed firms whose primary business strategy involves holding significant quantities of digital assets, such as bitcoin or ethereum , on their corporate balance sheets to drive shareholder value. Companies in this space include Strategy , Strive, and Twenty One Capital.

"DATs have exacerbated the problem," said Sheikh of Cordoba Advisory Partners. When bitcoin is rising, these companies borrow money in the debt market or raise capital to buy more bitcoin, which magnifies the upswings. They have also sold bitcoin to make their bond coupon payments. "It leads to enormous volatility on the upside and downside," Sheikh said.

As of mid-November, Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, holds 850,849 BTC, according to a regulatory filing . That represents roughly 4% of bitcoin's total supply. The company acquired these holdings at a total cost of approximately $64.2 billion, with an average purchase price of roughly $75,452 per coin, according to the filing.

Bitcoin has been trending lower since the peak in October 2025. A trading range has taken hold and the bottom of the range is just below 60,000, said Katie Stockton, founder and managing partner of Fairlead Strategies. "It appears to be trying to find a footing," she said.

Oversold conditions on the heels of recent lows in June and July, in addition to long-term momentum, suggest bitcoin can support an upturn, she said. But that depends on whether the crypto can hold at a current range around $60,000, she said. "At the end of the day, bitcoin is exceptionally volatile. extraction.body: Bitcoin 's latest sell-off is reviving doubts that it can behave as the "digital gold" market hedge that crypto backers have long envisioned. Coming into 2026, experts said that showing bitcoin could serve as a market hedge rather than a risk-on asset that moves up and down with growth stocks was an important test for the cryptocurrency. Bitcoin was trading under $62,000 on Friday morning, down from an all-time high of more than $126,000 in early October last year. Its downward spiral in recent months and weeks has been precipitated by a confluence of factors. The heavy midterm elections losses for the Republicans, the Binance hack, and a world on edge about the security of all things technology — FAA ground stop, the outage of the National Security Agency's highly classified internal communications system, several online banking outages — have not helped the mood when it comes to putting trust in the digital world. But the market itself may be the biggest factor. Investors are currently in sell everything mode, including tech stocks and gold — the Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 tumbled into correction territory on Friday, according to CNBC data. Bitcoin's recent price action has also tracked the move in the biggest tech IPOs , SpaceX and Anthropic. Taken together, the cryptocurrency is failing the test again when it comes to showing its worth as a market hedge during times of investor anxiety. In the past month alone, bitcoin had dropped roughly $20,000, as of Friday morning, according to CNBC data. Investors and financial management firms aren't viewing it as safe an investment as in the past, said Ryan Kirkley, co-founder and chief executive of Global Settlement Network, a Miami-based fintech that provides infrastructure for currency settlement, including crypto. "There's a bit more caution than there was a year ago." What is behind bitcoin's fall, and what is in store for its future? Here is what experts say. There have been many theories about how bitcoin would react based on different market and economic conditions. But historically, bitcoin has done best in low-rate environments and when lending opportunities are plentiful, said Juan Xavier Sanchez, head of wealth strategy at Activest Wealth Management in Aventura, Florida. When rates are down and treasuries aren't paying good yields, people tend to be more risk-seeking for higher returns. "Bitcoin for many investors is in that bucket," Sanchez said. Experts have noted that gold, which is now down over 35% from its early 2026 peak, is less attractive when cash accounts are paying 5%. Investments like gold and bitcoin offer no yield. Bitcoin's rising correlation with the Nasdaq-100 since late September suggests the two are increasingly moving in tandem, according to data from Fairlead Strategies, a technical research firm. That's consistent with an environment of higher volatility in which correlations across risk assets tend to increase. However, the correlation remains below its early-2026 highs, the data show. Bitcoin has certain characteristics of digital gold, in that it has a limited supply, no single owner and no CEO or board that can decide to issue more, said Anthony Georgiades, founder and general partner at Innovating Capital in New York, which invests in early-stage crypto, blockchain, digital infrastructure and deep tech companies. But it's also been caught up in monetary policy since its inception. The last decade or so of monetary policy has been extremely rewarding to speculative risk-on assets, Georgiades said. However, in periods of volatility, those types of assets have experienced the most significant drawdowns and have been the most heavily punished, Georgiades said. That means that a shock on one side of the board that might be completely independent of bitcoin could trigger a large volatility event "given how intertwined digital assets have become in the overall financial system," he said. Notably, bitcoin hasn't acted much like digital gold in more recent years, said Abe Sheikh, chief investment officer of Cordoba Advisory Partners in New York. In fact, it has fallen substantially during periods when the stock market has been falling. For example, from October 6 through November 18, the S&P 500 fell about 6.3%, and bitcoin fell around 27%. From January 21, 2025 through April 8, 2025, the S&P dropped around 17.4%, while bitcoin slid 27.8%, he said. Democrats gaining control over both houses is viewed as a negative for crypto from a market perspective. The crypto industry spent more than $200 million to support crypto-friendly candidates, but its role had less of an impact on overall results than in the last election cycle. However, bitcoin's downward trend was already in the works, said Cyrus Amini, chief investment officer at Hyphen Wealth Management in Lafayette, California. In September, the Clarity Act failed in the U.S. Senate, and while its outlook is now dim , according to many political and market experts, some form of crypto legislation is still considered a priority for many Democrats and Republicans, while the Trump-appointed heads of the Commodity Future Trading Commission and Securities and Exchange Commission continue to favor crypto in rulemaking. This fall, investors also started to question the security of encryption technology, leading to more concerns over the security of their bitcoin holdings, said Kirkley of Global Settlement Network. The Binance hack in October muddied the waters further. And the recent stock market jitters and economic concerns piled on doubts, Kirkley said. The last few weeks have been especially rough with data security concerns from multiple fronts, he added. Wall Street's embrace of bitcoin has been a big positive for the cryptocurrency. Kirkley noted that 20% of bitcoin's market price is coming from institutional investors, and that's a conservative estimate. In addition, new research from digital assets company Galaxy shows that a record 40.5% of all 13F-reported spot bitcoin exchange-traded product holdings, and 11.2% of all the bitcoin in the funds, came from advisory and wealth planning firms, such as RIAs and brokerage platforms, as of the third quarter 13F filings with the SEC, which are required of firms with over $100 million in assets to report their holdings. Much of this investment is through bitcoin spot ETFs like the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) that track its price. These ETFs, first approved by the SEC in January 2024, were supposed to provide a reliable new source of institutional demand. But ETF ownership also makes bitcoin especially easy to sell. Outflows from several of these funds have been substantial in recent months. IBIT, the largest of its peers, had six-month net outflows of $1.65 billion through Nov. 18 and one-month outflows of $1.37 billion, according to ETF Database. The second biggest, Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC ) had one-month net outflows of $322.65 million and six-month net outflows of $771.86 million, according to ETF Database. Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ( BTC ) had one-month net outflows of $66.35 million, though it had inflows of $590.04 million over six months. As of September 2026, public companies collectively hold close to 1.29 million bitcoins, which is more than 6% of the 21 million coins in existence, according to bitcoin.com . Most public companies invest their corporate treasury portfolios in low-risk, highly liquid instruments such as money market funds, Treasury bonds and Treasury bills. That said, there are some well-known companies that have invested in bitcoin. SpaceX, for example, purchased 18,712 bitcoins for a total cost of $661 million, at an average price of $35,324 per coin. The company began accumulating bitcoin in early 2021 and held its position unchanged from mid-2024 until its IPO filing . Digital Asset Treasury companies, known as DATs or DATCOs, have also played a role in bitcoin's volatility . DATs are publicly listed firms whose primary business strategy involves holding significant quantities of digital assets, such as bitcoin or ethereum , on their corporate balance sheets to drive shareholder value. Companies in this space include Strategy , Strive, and Twenty One Capital. "DATs have exacerbated the problem," said Sheikh of Cordoba Advisory Partners. When bitcoin is rising, these companies borrow money in the debt market or raise capital to buy more bitcoin, which magnifies the upswings. They have also sold bitcoin to make their bond coupon payments. "It leads to enormous volatility on the upside and downside," Sheikh said. As of mid-November, Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, holds 850,849 BTC, according to a regulatory filing . That represents roughly 4% of bitcoin's total supply. The company acquired these holdings at a total cost of approximately $64.2 billion, with an average purchase price of roughly $75,452 per coin, according to the filing. Bitcoin has been trending lower since the peak in October 2025. A trading range has taken hold and the bottom of the range is just below 60,000, said Katie Stockton, founder and managing partner of Fairlead Strategies. "It appears to be trying to find a footing," she said. Oversold conditions on the heels of recent lows in June and July, in addition to long-term momentum, suggest bitcoin can support an upturn, she said. But that depends on whether the crypto can hold at a current range around $60,000, she said. "At the end of the day, bitcoin is exceptionally volatile. It's still an area that people might go to sell when they think that risk is higher in other areas." By mid-morning Friday, the price of bitcoin had slipped below $60,000, its lowest mark since July. It was on pace for its seventh-straight weekly loss for the first time since May 2022, according to CNBC data.

Bitcoin has certain characteristics of digital gold, in that it has a limited supply, no single owner and no CEO or board that can decide to issue more, said Anthony Georgiades, founder and general partner at Innovating Capital in New York, which invests in early-stage crypto, blockchain, digital infrastructure and deep tech companies.

But it's also been caught up in monetary policy since its inception. The last decade or so of monetary policy has been extremely rewarding to speculative risk-on assets, Georgiades said. However, in periods of volatility, those types of assets have experienced the most significant drawdowns and have been the most heavily punished, Georgiades said. That means that a shock on one side of the board that might be completely independent of bitcoin could trigger a large volatility event "given how intertwined digital assets have become in the overall financial system," he said.

Notably, bitcoin hasn't acted much like digital gold in more recent years, said Abe Sheikh, chief investment officer of Cordoba Advisory Partners in New York. In fact, it has fallen substantially during periods when the stock market has been falling. For example, from October 6 through November 18, the S&P 500 fell about 6.3%, and bitcoin fell around 27%. From January 21, 2025 through April 8, 2025, the S&P dropped around 17.4%, while bitcoin slid 27.8%, he said.

Democrats gaining control over both houses is viewed as a negative for crypto from a market perspective. The crypto industry spent more than $200 million to support crypto-friendly candidates, but its role had less of an impact on overall results than in the last election cycle. However, bitcoin's downward trend was already in the works, said Cyrus Amini, chief investment officer at Hyphen Wealth Management in Lafayette, California.

In September, the Clarity Act failed in the U.S. Senate, and while its outlook is now dim , according to many political and market experts, some form of crypto legislation is still considered a priority for many Democrats and Republicans, while the Trump-appointed heads of the Commodity Future Trading Commission and Securities and Exchange Commission continue to favor crypto in rulemaking.

This fall, investors also started to question the security of encryption technology, leading to more concerns over the security of their bitcoin holdings, said Kirkley of Global Settlement Network. The Binance hack in October muddied the waters further. And the recent stock market jitters and economic concerns piled on doubts, Kirkley said. The last few weeks have been especially rough with data security concerns from multiple fronts, he added.

Wall Street's embrace of bitcoin has been a big positive for the cryptocurrency. Kirkley noted that 20% of bitcoin's market price is coming from institutional investors, and that's a conservative estimate.

In addition, new research from digital assets company Galaxy shows that a record 40.5% of all 13F-reported spot bitcoin exchange-traded product holdings, and 11.2% of all the bitcoin in the funds, came from advisory and wealth planning firms, such as RIAs and brokerage platforms, as of the third quarter 13F filings with the SEC, which are required of firms with over $100 million in assets to report their holdings.

Much of this investment is through bitcoin spot ETFs like the iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) that track its price. These ETFs, first approved by the SEC in January 2024, were supposed to provide a reliable new source of institutional demand. But ETF ownership also makes bitcoin especially easy to sell.

Outflows from several of these funds have been substantial in recent months. IBIT, the largest of its peers, had six-month net outflows of $1.65 billion through Nov. 18 and one-month outflows of $1.37 billion, according to ETF Database. The second biggest, Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund ( FBTC ) had one-month net outflows of $322.65 million and six-month net outflows of $771.86 million, according to ETF Database. Grayscale Bitcoin Mini Trust ETF ( BTC ) had one-month net outflows of $66.35 million, though it had inflows of $590.04 million over six months.
As of September 2026, public companies collectively hold close to 1.29 million bitcoins, which is more than 6% of the 21 million coins in existence, according to bitcoin.com .

Most public companies invest their corporate treasury portfolios in low-risk, highly liquid instruments such as money market funds, Treasury bonds and Treasury bills. That said, there are some well-known companies that have invested in bitcoin. SpaceX, for example, purchased 18,712 bitcoins for a total cost of $661 million, at an average price of $35,324 per coin. The company began accumulating bitcoin in early 2021 and held its position unchanged from mid-2024 until its IPO filing .

Digital Asset Treasury companies, known as DATs or DATCOs, have also played a role in bitcoin's volatility . DATs are publicly listed firms whose primary business strategy involves holding significant quantities of digital assets, such as bitcoin or ethereum , on their corporate balance sheets to drive shareholder value. Companies in this space include Strategy , Strive, and Twenty One Capital.

"DATs have exacerbated the problem," said Sheikh of Cordoba Advisory Partners. When bitcoin is rising, these companies borrow money in the debt market or raise capital to buy more bitcoin, which magnifies the upswings. They have also sold bitcoin to make their bond coupon payments. "It leads to enormous volatility on the upside and downside," Sheikh said.

As of mid-November, Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, holds 850,849 BTC, according to a regulatory filing . That represents roughly 4% of bitcoin's total supply. The company acquired these holdings at a total cost of approximately $64.2 billion, with an average purchase price of roughly $75,452 per coin, according to the filing.

Bitcoin has been trending lower since the peak in October 2025. A trading range has taken hold and the bottom of the range is just below 60,000, said Katie Stockton, founder and managing partner of Fairlead Strategies. "It appears to be trying to find a footing," she said.

Oversold conditions on the heels of recent lows in June and July, in addition to long-term momentum, suggest bitcoin can support an upturn, she said. But that depends on whether the crypto can hold at a current range around $60,000, she said. "At the end of the day, bitcoin is exceptionally volatile. It's still an area that people might go to sell when they think that risk is higher in other areas."

By mid-morning Friday, the price of bitcoin had slipped below $60,000, its lowest mark since July. It was on pace for its seventh-straight weekly loss for the first time since May 2022, according to CNBC data.

Taken together, the cryptocurrency is failing the test again when it comes to showing its worth as a market hedge during times of investor anxiety.

extraction.body: Bitcoin fell sharply on Thursday, dropping below $85,000 for the first time in nearly two months, as a broad pullback in risk assets swept through global markets and intensified pressure on cryptocurrencies. The world’s largest digital asset slid as much as 5.7% to $84,233, its lowest level since Dec. 1. The decline marked a significant breakdown after weeks of sideways trading and underscored the fragility of sentiment across the crypto market. Losses were even steeper among smaller tokens, with Ether, XRP, Dogecoin, Cardano and Solana all falling by 6% or more. The sharp move lower in prices triggered a wave of forced selling across crypto derivatives markets. Around $785 million worth of digital assets were liquidated over the past 24 hours, according to data compiled by Coinglass. More than half of those liquidations occurred in just the last four hours, reflecting the speed at which losses cascaded as key technical levels were breached. The latest drop extended a broader downturn that has persisted in crypto markets since early October. Bitcoin prices had largely stagnated in recent weeks, even as technology stocks and precious metals such as gold and silver rallied. That divergence broke down abruptly, however, as cryptocurrencies began to mirror a wider selloff in risk assets. Technology stocks led the decline, with Microsoft shares collapsing more than 11%, a move that would rank as their worst one-day fall since March 2020. The selloff followed the company’s report of slowing growth in its cloud business and dragged the Nasdaq Composite lower by roughly 1.5%, reinforcing a risk-off tone across markets. The pressure was not limited to equities. Precious metals, which had surged to record highs, also reversed violently. Gold, which had briefly climbed above $5,600 per ounce earlier in the session — having never traded above $5,000 before Sunday night — plunged nearly 10% within minutes during US morning trade, falling back below $5,200. Silver followed a similar trajectory, sliding from around $121 per ounce to $108. Bitcoin exchange-traded funds have also come under strain. So far this week, bitcoin ETFs have recorded $160.1 million in net outflows, according to data from SoSoValue, extending a pattern of capital leaving the products amid market turbulence. Julio Moreno, head of research at CryptoQuant, said the recent pullback represents the first meaningful stress test for bitcoin ETFs since their rapid growth last year. Moreno noted that cumulative ETF flows peaked at $72.6 billion on Oct. 10, 2025, and have since seen $6.1 billion in net outflows. That reduction has cut ETF holdings to about $66.5 billion, representing an 8.4% drawdown from the peak. “If price holds above ETF realized price, it gives this cohort a reason to stay invested. If it fails, ETF flows risk shifting from passive consolidation into active distribution. Right now, Bitcoin is trading at the line where ETF conviction is tested,” Moreno wrote.
