When Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) reported on Nov. 17, its fiscal third-quarter revenue had more than doubled from the year before, to a record $115.8 billion. But for memory investors, the more telling number was how much the artificial intelligence (AI) chip leader has agreed to pay its suppliers. Nvidia 's supply commitments rose to $390 billion, up from $279 billion a quarter earlier. And the company said the increase was "primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply." Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » That's good news for Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) , one of the three big makers of the memory chips Nvidia buys. But Micron stock is around $702 as I write, about 42% under the record $1,213.56 it closed at on June 25. I think the market's underrating what Nvidia's report says about Micron's business. Showing how fast its buying has picked up, Nvidia's supply commitments have more than tripled over two quarters. They were at $119 billion as of April 26, climbed to $279 billion by July 26, and hit $390 billion by Oct. 25, the end of its fiscal third quarter. In both of the last two quarters, the company linked most of the rise to memory. What's more, the money's coming due sooner. Of the $390 billion, $203 billion falls in Nvidia's fiscal 2028, which ends in January 2028. Three months earlier, that year's figure was $87 billion. In short, Nvidia is locking in memory long before it needs the chips, and much of this spending will probably land within about a year. Nvidia doesn't say how it splits the spending between its memory suppliers. SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics sell Nvidia high-bandwidth memory (HBM), too. (HBM is the stacked memory that sits next to AI processors.) Micron doesn't name its largest buyers, either. However, no single customer made up 10% or more of its revenue for its fiscal 2026, which ended Sept. 3, down from one customer at 17% the year before. So Micron's direct sales to Nvidia, whatever they are, were under a tenth of its revenue last year. What Micron does say is encouraging. It's working with Nvidia on what it calls the industry's first custom HBM4E chip, designed for Nvidia's next generation of graphics processing units . And its cloud memory business unit, which sells HBM to all data center customers, keeps growing. It pulled in $16.3 billion of revenue in the three months ended Sept. 3, up 18% from the previous quarter and more than triple the $4.5 billion of a year before, with an 83% gross margin. On its fiscal fourth-quarter call, Micron said it had lifted its HBM prices significantly for calendar 2027. Nvidia's commitments look like the buyer's side of a change Micron is already building its business around. Micron has now signed 26 multiyear strategic customer agreements, up from 16 a quarter earlier. All are take-or-pay deals, so customers commit to buying fixed volumes and can lose deposits if they fall short. Customers have committed $32 billion under the deals, mainly as cash deposits, compared to the $22 billion Micron forecast a quarter before. Micron also puts its remaining performance obligations (contracted sales it hasn't recognized yet) at around $150 billion, counting just committed volumes at minimum prices. "[E]ven at floor prices, we expect margins meaningfully above any prior cycle peak margins," chief financial officer Mark Murphy said in Micron's prepared remarks for the fiscal fourth quarter. But the stock trades like the boom might end soon. At around $702, Micron's price-to-earnings ratio is about 4 based on analysts' estimates for fiscal 2027 (which ends next September), and only about 9 on fiscal 2026's actual earnings of $74.33 per share. A price like that suggests investors expect profits to dive before long. Sure, memory prices have crashed before, and Micron plans to spend more on new plant space, which might loosen supply in late 2028 and beyond. But a growing share of its sales now comes with committed volumes, deposits, and price floors, protections Micron didn't have in past memory busts. When Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA) reported on Nov. 17, its fiscal third-quarter revenue had more than doubled from the year before, to a record $115.8 billion. But for memory investors, the more telling number was how much the artificial intelligence (AI) chip leader has agreed to pay its suppliers.
Nvidia 's supply commitments rose to $390 billion, up from $279 billion a quarter earlier. And the company said the increase was "primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply."

Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

That's good news for Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) , one of the three big makers of the memory chips Nvidia buys. But Micron stock is around $702 as I write, about 42% under the record $1,213.56 it closed at on June 25.
I think the market's underrating what Nvidia's report says about Micron's business.

Showing how fast its buying has picked up, Nvidia's supply commitments have more than tripled over two quarters. They were at $119 billion as of April 26, climbed to $279 billion by July 26, and hit $390 billion by Oct. 25, the end of its fiscal third quarter. In both of the last two quarters, the company linked most of the rise to memory. What's more, the money's coming due sooner. Of the $390 billion, $203 billion falls in Nvidia's fiscal 2028, which ends in January 2028. Three months earlier, that year's figure was $87 billion.
In short, Nvidia is locking in memory long before it needs the chips, and much of this spending will probably land within about a year.

Nvidia doesn't say how it splits the spending between its memory suppliers. SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics sell Nvidia high-bandwidth memory (HBM), too. (HBM is the stacked memory that sits next to AI processors.)
Micron doesn't name its largest buyers, either. However, no single customer made up 10% or more of its revenue for its fiscal 2026, which ended Sept. 3, down from one customer at 17% the year before.
So Micron's direct sales to Nvidia, whatever they are, were under a tenth of its revenue last year.
What Micron does say is encouraging. It's working with Nvidia on what it calls the industry's first custom HBM4E chip, designed for Nvidia's next generation of graphics processing units .

And its cloud memory business unit, which sells HBM to all data center customers, keeps growing. It pulled in $16.3 billion of revenue in the three months ended Sept. 3, up 18% from the previous quarter and more than triple the $4.5 billion of a year before, with an 83% gross margin. On its fiscal fourth-quarter call, Micron said it had lifted its HBM prices significantly for calendar 2027.
Nvidia's commitments look like the buyer's side of a change Micron is already building its business around.

Micron has now signed 26 multiyear strategic customer agreements, up from 16 a quarter earlier. All are take-or-pay deals, so customers commit to buying fixed volumes and can lose deposits if they fall short.
Customers have committed $32 billion under the deals, mainly as cash deposits, compared to the $22 billion Micron forecast a quarter before.

Micron also puts its remaining performance obligations (contracted sales it hasn't recognized yet) at around $150 billion, counting just committed volumes at minimum prices. "[E]ven at floor prices, we expect margins meaningfully above any prior cycle peak margins," chief financial officer Mark Murphy said in Micron's prepared remarks for the fiscal fourth quarter.

But the stock trades like the boom might end soon. At around $702, Micron's price-to-earnings ratio is about 4 based on analysts' estimates for fiscal 2027 (which ends next September), and only about 9 on fiscal 2026's actual earnings of $74.33 per share. A price like that suggests investors expect profits to dive before long.

Sure, memory prices have crashed before, and Micron plans to spend more on new plant space, which might loosen supply in late 2028 and beyond. But a growing share of its sales now comes with committed volumes, deposits, and price floors, protections Micron didn't have in past memory busts.

In many ways, Taiwan Semiconductor , or TSMC, is the gatekeeper of the AI boom, because without it, the breakneck growth of Nvidia, Micron, and other AI-related companies would not be possible. TSMC does pretty much one thing: It makes chips and semiconductor components for other companies, like Nvidia and Micron. That's why it is called a foundry -- a term that refers to a factory where things are manufactured. As a semiconductor foundry, it is dominant, making about 70% of all chips and roughly 90% of more advanced AI semiconductor chips. Its major customers include Nvidia, as well as other tech stock giants like Apple , Broadcom , Advanced Micro Devices , and Amazon , to name a few. TSMC makes millions of advanced chips every year and will generate some $33 billion from its largest customer, Nvidia, in 2026. Nvidia could not produce that many advanced chips that quickly without TSMC. Its technologies and processes set it apart from competitors, and it stands alone in its ability to make the most advanced chips at such scale, speed, and cost. This is why Taiwan Semiconductor is so indispensable to Nvidia. TSMC does not play the same role for Micron, but it is just as valuable to the memory chipmaker. While TSMC doesn't make memory chips for Micron, it makes the components that are required for Micron's advanced, next-generation high bandwidth memory (HBM) chips, which are used for AI applications. As with Nvidia, TSMC's advanced technologies and processes are needed for these faster, more advanced HBM chips, and Micron could not make them as quickly or at such a scale without TSMC. In addition, Micron partners with TSMC to package the next-generation HBM chips using TSMC's CoWoS (chip-on-wafer-on-substrate) technology. Nvidia and other chip companies use TSMC packaging for their AI processors, which includes essential foundational wafers, or base dies, provided by TSMC to make the stack function. Micron signed an agreement with TSMC to produce the base die for these stacks, enabling them to adopt this architecture alongside Nvidia and others. So, without its connections to TSMC, it would not have access to the advanced components for its next-generation memory chips nor to TSMC's AI architecture stacks. passages: Nvidia 's supply commitments rose to $390 billion, up from $279 billion a quarter earlier.
And the company said the increase was "primarily related to the multi-year procurement of memory supply."
In both of the last two quarters, the company linked most of the rise to memory.
Three months earlier, that year's figure was $87 billion.
Of the three companies selling Nvidia its memory, Micron is the one I'd buy.
It's working with Nvidia on custom HBM, and unlike Samsung, it's a pure memory and storage business.
Micron's customers have made $32 billion in financial commitments under its multiyear supply deals.
Nvidia's commitments look like the buyer's side of a change Micron is already building its business around.
Sure, memory prices have crashed before, and Micron plans to spend more on new plant space, which might loosen supply in late 2028 and beyond.
But a growing share of its sales now comes with committed volumes, deposits, and price floors, protections Micron didn't have in past memory busts.
Micron also puts its remaining performance obligations (contracted sales it hasn't recognized yet) at around $150 billion, counting just committed volumes at minimum prices.
Nvidia doesn't say how it splits the spending between its memory suppliers.
SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics sell Nvidia high-bandwidth memory (HBM), too. (HBM is the stacked memory that sits next to AI processors.)
So Micron's direct sales to Nvidia, whatever they are, were under a tenth of its revenue last year.
The Motley Fool has positions in and recommends Micron Technology and Nvidia.
I think the market's underrating what Nvidia's report says about Micron's business.
In short, Nvidia is locking in memory long before it needs the chips, and much of this spending will probably land within about a year.

An attacker could send media from an attacker-controlled URL in a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message. When WhatsApp displayed that message in a thread, the attacker could learn the target's IP address. WhatsApp said someone may have used the flaw with specific spam messages. The company's security team discovered and reported the issue. A WhatsApp spokesperson said the team found the flaw while disrupting a scam campaign and believes a scammer used it to make scam messages seem more credible. WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity or whether those efforts succeeded. The second flaw, CVE-2026-102769, is an SQL injection vulnerability in WhatsApp for Android before version 2.26.35.74. It occurs when a recipient taps a crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial client. The tap can delete files stored on the device. An attacker could learn one bit about the user's chat database through an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel if the user is online when the malicious message arrives. WhatsApp said it found no evidence that anyone exploited the flaw in the wild. The third flaw, CVE-2026-44908, is a trust-validation vulnerability in WhatsApp's certificate verification mechanism for Meta AI's confidential computing infrastructure. It affects WhatsApp for iOS before version 2.26.24.72, WhatsApp Business for iOS and WhatsApp for Mac Desktop before version 2.26.23.72, WhatsApp for Android before version 2.26.23.74, and WhatsApp Business for Android before version 2.26.23.70. An actor positioned inside Meta infrastructure could bypass the hardware root of trust with a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key (VCEK) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key. Someone would first need to publish that certificate to the third-party binary transparency ledger that WhatsApp Private Processing uses. WhatsApp said the ledger shows every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, which confirms no exploitation. WhatsApp advises users to keep apps and devices updated. extraction.body: Meta-owned WhatsApp has addressed security vulnerabilities, including one impacting its Android app that it suspects may have been exploited in connection with scam messages. The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-23871 , has been described as a case of incomplete validation of external ad-reply URLs in WhatsApp for Android and WhatsApp Business for Android before 2.26.17.4. The issue could have "caused a target's device to reveal its IP information to an attacker if an attacker sent media from an attacker-controlled URL when a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message was rendered and displayed in a message thread," WhatsApp said. The messaging platform said it may have been "abused in conjunction with specific spam messages." Internal researchers on the WhatsApp Security Team have been credited with discovering and reporting the issue. When reached for comment, a WhatsApp spokesperson told The Hacker News that the vulnerability was discovered while disrupting a scam campaign. "We believe a scammer was using it to make their scam message seem more credible," the spokesperson added. WhatsApp did not disclose the scale of the activity, and if those efforts were successful. Also addressed by the company are two other flaws - Interestingly, CVE-2026-102769 is also capable of leaking one bit of information through a timing-based side channel if the user is online at the time of receipt of the malicious message. It "leaked one bit of information asked by the attacker about the user's chat database via an induced-crash delivery receipt timing side channel," WhatsApp added. There is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild. Successful exploitation of CVE-2026-44908, on the other hand, could have allowed a bad actor positioned within Meta infrastructure to bypass the hardware root of trust using a Versioned Chip Endorsement Key ( VCEK ) certificate not signed by the hardware manufacturer's key. "Any such VCEK Cert would first have to be published to the third-party binary transparency ledger used by WhatsApp Private Processing," WhatsApp noted. "The ledger shows that every published VCEK certificate chains to the hardware root of trust, confirming no exploitation." WhatsApp is advising users to keep their apps and devices up to date to ensure optimal protection. The company also said that it continuously works to strengthen its systems and acknowledged the bug bounty community's contributions towards keeping the platform secure. extraction.body: Crypto investors are hunting for the next positive catalyst after U.S. crypto regulation — a longtime market driver — fizzled in 2026. Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September. Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost. "Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager. He pointed to statements from the asset management giant's CEO, Larry Fink, who said the next major evolution in global finance is the creation of digital representations of every stock, bond, fund and real-world asset onto a shared blockchain ledger. Bitcoin traded around $61,500 on Friday, a more than 50% decline from its all-time high above $126,000 reached in October 2025. The broader digital asset market has struggled after the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, failed to advance in the Senate in September. Investors now see Wall Street's embrace of blockchain technology — particularly tokenization — as the next trend to give bitcoin a boost. "Every single traditional firm is now looking at digital assets," BitGo CEO Mike Belshe told CNBC last week in an exclusive interview from the fintech-focused Cantor Convergence conference in Miami Beach. That includes BlackRock , the world's largest asset manager. He pointed to statements from the asset management giant's CEO, Larry Fink, who said the next major evolution in global finance is the creation of digital representations of every stock, bond, fund and real-world asset onto a shared blockchain ledger. "I think the biggest catalyst we're seeing right now is actually very much in motion and it's happening, which is capital markets are moving onchain," eToro CEO Yoni Assia told CNBC in an exclusive interview from the conference. He pointed to the SpaceX IPO as an example, which had derivatives trading on eToro before the IPO. "First day of trading, we distributed it to our retail clients, and it started trading 24/7, and that's all because capital markets are now copying crypto markets and are sitting on the same rails," Assia said. "Crypto markets have always been 24/7, they never sleep, and now what we're seeing is that capital markets are copying crypto markets using the same technology so stocks are moving onchain, they're being tokenized." Assia said that supportive regulation in the U.S. from agencies, including the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, is also helping adoption of crypto. He pointed to the CFTC earlier this month clearing the way for crypto-style perpetual futures tied to individual stocks to trade on regulated U.S. exchanges for the first time. Assia also highlighted the SEC's move to issue an order in September, creating a regulatory pathway for certain trading venues to trade tokenized representations of publicly traded U.S. stocks. "Blockchain technology is now starting to power what's happening in capital markets," Assia told CNBC. "That is the one of the biggest changes we're going to see in capital markets for many, many years." "We're talking about hundreds of trillions of dollars that are going to be tokenized and move onchain and at the same time, I do believe that will support prices of bitcoin and other blockchains as well," he continued. The industry is also watching whether inflation will ease and geopolitical tensions will subside in the new year, which could lower broader macro risk currently hampering the industry. Last month, Strategy's Michael Saylor said he thinks bitcoin's next bull market is already underway. ARK Invest Chief Investment Officer Cathie Wood told CNBC the investment management firm's $1.5 million bull case price target for bitcoin by 2030 still stands. She also said that it wouldn't surprise her if bitcoin reached its all-time high again before the end of 2027. "Our macro forecast has inflation breaking down considerably," Wood told CNBC in an exclusive interview at Cantor Convergence. "I think the elections have increased our confidence there because the war [in Iran], one way or the other, is going to end." She added that "bitcoin has weathered so much bad news," including the $6.3 billion Binance hack and the "distraction" of AI which, "many people would say is sucking the oxygen away from bitcoin." The maturation of the artificial intelligence trade could provide an opportunity for bitcoin to find new inflows. Wood said that ARK Invest believes bitcoin has found its low and stressed that cybersecurity is "top of mind right now," which could provide yet another opportunity for crypto markets to rebound. "I think if the Bitcoin and crypto world coalesces and makes investors feel that they've got their arms around security and actually understand that there might be more security issues in the traditional financial system, I think we're going to see a wave of support," Wood said. sources.title: Nothing's new device to launch 8 December, but what is it? It's not a phone, headphones or a speaker– we know that much - Yahoo Tech
passages: While there's no confirmation on that, the company has informed T3 that all will be revealed on 8 December 2026 – a week after Black Friday .
Still, considering Nothing's reluctance to keeping secrets, we're sure that we'll hear more about this new launch in the coming days.
Nothing founder Carl Pei recently teased a new device that won't feature a "new screen", nor was it possible to build as an app.

Either way, the Nothing AI device is an interesting prospect – not least as it's launching at a strange time for an industry that tends to avoid the holiday season for the announcement of new products.
Nothing has also been rumoured to be working on its own smart glasses too, like the Ray-Ban Meta pairs.
What it won't be is the Nothing Phone (4), although that could also see the firm switch more to an AI-centric operating system in future.

extraction.body: Nothing founder Carl Pei recently teased a new device that won't feature a "new screen", nor was it possible to build as an app. So, what has his firm got up its sleeve? While there's no confirmation on that, the company has informed T3 that all will be revealed on 8 December 2026 – a week after Black Friday . All we know for now is that it will be an "AI device" and has been designed around "the context gap" – use cases for the AI systems we already have access to. The brand has also released a new teaser image, which looks a bit like a camera lens. Maybe the new device is an AI pin, a bit like the Plaud Note Pin or Meta's Muse Charm. Except this could also have a camera to peer at the outside world to add "context" to your requests and queries. Nothing has also been rumoured to be working on its own smart glasses too, like the Ray-Ban Meta pairs. That could also be a possibility. What it won't be is the Nothing Phone (4), although that could also see the firm switch more to an AI-centric operating system in future. Pei himself suggested a while back that he sees phones moving away from apps and more to agentic AI. Either way, the Nothing AI device is an interesting prospect – not least as it's launching at a strange time for an industry that tends to avoid the holiday season for the announcement of new products. In the west, at least. Chinese phone manufacturers are known to get ahead of rivals by unveiling new handsets at the end of each year – but mainly for China only. Still, considering Nothing's reluctance to keeping secrets, we're sure that we'll hear more about this new launch in the coming days. Expect a new tease or two, anyway.

Either way, the Nothing AI device is an interesting prospect – not least as it's launching at a strange time for an industry that tends to avoid the holiday season for the announcement of new products. In the west, at least.

facts.text: While there's no confirmation on that, the company has informed T3 that all will be revealed on 8 December 2026 – a week after Black Friday .
Still, considering Nothing's reluctance to keeping secrets, we're sure that we'll hear more about this new launch in the coming days.
Nothing founder Carl Pei recently teased a new device that won't feature a "new screen", nor was it possible to build as an app.

Either way, the Nothing AI device is an interesting prospect – not least as it's launching at a strange time for an industry that tends to avoid the holiday season for the announcement of new products.
Nothing has also been rumoured to be working on its own smart glasses too, like the Ray-Ban Meta pairs.
What it won't be is the Nothing Phone (4), although that could also see the firm switch more to an AI-centric operating system in future.

extraction.body: Nothing founder Carl Pei recently teased a new device that won't feature a "new screen", nor was it possible to build as an app. So, what has his firm got up its sleeve? While there's no confirmation on that, the company has informed T3 that all will be revealed on 8 December 2026 – a week after Black Friday . All we know for now is that it will be an "AI device" and has been designed around "the context gap" – use cases for the AI systems we already have access to. The brand has also released a new teaser image, which looks a bit like a camera lens. Maybe the new device is an AI pin, a bit like the Plaud Note Pin or Meta's Muse Charm. Except this could also have a camera to peer at the outside world to add "context" to your requests and queries. Nothing has also been rumoured to be working on its own smart glasses too, like the Ray-Ban Meta pairs. That could also be a possibility. What it won't be is the Nothing Phone (4), although that could also see the firm switch more to an AI-centric operating system in future. Pei himself suggested a while back that he sees phones moving away from apps and more to agentic AI. Either way, the Nothing AI device is an interesting prospect – not least as it's launching at a strange time for an industry that tends to avoid the holiday season for the announcement of new products. In the west, at least. Chinese phone manufacturers are known to get ahead of rivals by unveiling new handsets at the end of each year – but mainly for China only. Still, considering Nothing's reluctance to keeping secrets, we're sure that we'll hear more about this new launch in the coming days. Expect a new tease or two, anyway.

Here’s how it works . Nothing founder Carl Pei recently teased a new device that won't feature a "new screen", nor was it possible to build as an app. So, what has his firm got up its sleeve? While there's no confirmation on that, the company has informed T3 that all will be revealed on 8 December 2026 – a week after Black Friday . All we know for now is that it will be an "AI device" and has been designed around "the context gap" – use cases for the AI systems we already have access to. The brand has also released a new teaser image, which looks a bit like a camera lens. Maybe the new device is an AI pin, a bit like the Plaud Note Pin or Meta's Muse Charm. Except this could also have a camera to peer at the outside world to add "context" to your requests and queries. Nothing has also been rumoured to be working on its own smart glasses too, like the Ray-Ban Meta pairs. That could also be a possibility. What it won't be is the Nothing Phone (4), although that could also see the firm switch more to an AI-centric operating system in future. Pei himself suggested a while back that he sees phones moving away from apps and more to agentic AI. Either way, the Nothing AI device is an interesting prospect – not least as it's launching at a strange time for an industry that tends to avoid the holiday season for the announcement of new products. In the west, at least. Nothing founder Carl Pei recently teased a new device that won't feature a "new screen", nor was it possible to build as an app. So, what has his firm got up its sleeve?
While there's no confirmation on that, the company has informed T3 that all will be revealed on 8 December 2026 – a week after Black Friday .
All we know for now is that it will be an "AI device" and has been designed around "the context gap" – use cases for the AI systems we already have access to.

The brand has also released a new teaser image, which looks a bit like a camera lens. Maybe the new device is an AI pin, a bit like the Plaud Note Pin or Meta's Muse Charm. Except this could also have a camera to peer at the outside world to add "context" to your requests and queries.
Nothing has also been rumoured to be working on its own smart glasses too, like the Ray-Ban Meta pairs. That could also be a possibility.

What it won't be is the Nothing Phone (4), although that could also see the firm switch more to an AI-centric operating system in future. Pei himself suggested a while back that he sees phones moving away from apps and more to agentic AI.

Either way, the Nothing AI device is an interesting prospect – not least as it's launching at a strange time for an industry that tends to avoid the holiday season for the announcement of new products. In the west, at least.

Still, considering Nothing's reluctance to keeping secrets, we're sure that we'll hear more about this new launch in the coming days. Expect a new tease or two, anyway.

extraction.body: The bitcoin price crashed below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, falling about $1,800 in roughly an hour as a deepening U.S. tech stock selloff dragged risk assets lower. Bitcoin traded near $61,400 at 9:40 a.m. ET and slid to about $59,600 by 10:45 a.m., a drop of nearly 3%, according to Look Into Bitcoin data . The bitcoin price is down about $3,400, or more than 5%, from the same time Thursday, when it traded near $63,000. The break of $60,000 is a key psychological level, and it came with little warning. Bitcoin price had held above $61,000 for most of the morning, even after a third straight daily loss. Wall Street opened sharply lower. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% in morning trading as shares of Anthropic extended losses in its second day since a record Nasdaq debut. Nvidia and AMD also traded lower. Bitcoin has been moving with tech stocks. The market has questioned whether heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and Friday’s open did nothing to ease that worry. Rate expectations are adding pressure. Traders see a roughly 94% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed . Higher rates tend to hurt bitcoin and other assets that pay no yield. Earlier Friday, South Korea’s Kospi index fell more than 5% and chipmakers sank across Asia. That selling carried into U.S. trading and then into bitcoin. Some analysts had flagged $60,000 as a floor. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies told CNBC the bottom of bitcoin’s trading range sits “just below 60,000,” and that it “appears to be trying to find a footing.” Friday’s drop tests that view. CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said this week the drop is a “continuation of the existing bear market.” His base case is range trading around $60,000 to $90,000 through much of 2027. JUST IN: Bitcoin falls below $60,000 for the first time since June. BTC is now less than 4% away from a new cycle low 👀 pic.twitter.com/GSZkbGdzZz Funds have been sellers. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost $541.1 million on Thursday, its biggest one-day outflow on record. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total, extending a streak of heavy withdrawals this week. Leveraged traders were hit as well. More than $700 million in crypto positions were liquidated in the 24 hours before the latest drop, and about 86% were bets on higher prices. The slide below $60,000 likely forced out more of them. The move extends a month-long slump. Bitcoin has dropped roughly $20,000 in the past month, a slide tracked as the price fell under $62,000 on Thursday. Crypto stocks fell even faster. Strategy (MSTR) was down about 7% near $79.85, a day after it tumbled for a sixth straight session . Coinbase (COIN) fell about 3% to $105.36. Shares of Strive (ASST) fell to $15.31 Friday morning, down 21.47%, or $4.19, over the past five days. The stock has slid steadily from near $19.50 as bitcoin price’s sell-off deepened, with its sharpest drop in Friday’s trading. Bitcoin miners took the worst of it. MARA Holdings (MARA) dropped about 11% to $5.55. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 11% to $15.85, and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell about 12% to $5.13. Data center operators that also mine bitcoin were hit hard. IREN fell about 12% to $12.62, and Cipher Digital (CIFR) dropped 14% to $5.58. Both have traded with AI stocks, which are also under pressure. The bitcoin price is now at its lowest since the first days of July. passages: The bitcoin price crashed below $60,000 on Friday for the first time since early July, falling about $1,800 in roughly an hour as a deepening U.S. tech stock selloff dragged risk assets lower.

Bitcoin traded near $61,400 at 9:40 a.m. ET and slid to about $59,600 by 10:45 a.m., a drop of nearly 3%, according to Look Into Bitcoin data . The bitcoin price is down about $3,400, or more than 5%, from the same time Thursday, when it traded near $63,000.
The break of $60,000 is a key psychological level, and it came with little warning. Bitcoin price had held above $61,000 for most of the morning, even after a third straight daily loss.

Wall Street opened sharply lower. The Nasdaq Composite fell more than 2% in morning trading as shares of Anthropic extended losses in its second day since a record Nasdaq debut. Nvidia and AMD also traded lower.
Bitcoin has been moving with tech stocks. The market has questioned whether heavy spending on artificial intelligence will pay off, and Friday’s open did nothing to ease that worry.

Rate expectations are adding pressure. Traders see a roughly 94% chance the Federal Reserve raises rates in December, CME Group’s FedWatch tool showed . Higher rates tend to hurt bitcoin and other assets that pay no yield.
Earlier Friday, South Korea’s Kospi index fell more than 5% and chipmakers sank across Asia. That selling carried into U.S. trading and then into bitcoin.

Some analysts had flagged $60,000 as a floor. Katie Stockton of Fairlead Strategies told CNBC the bottom of bitcoin’s trading range sits “just below 60,000,” and that it “appears to be trying to find a footing.” Friday’s drop tests that view.
CoinShares head of research James Butterfill said this week the drop is a “continuation of the existing bear market.” His base case is range trading around $60,000 to $90,000 through much of 2027.

Funds have been sellers. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) lost $541.1 million on Thursday, its biggest one-day outflow on record. U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $582 million in total, extending a streak of heavy withdrawals this week.

Leveraged traders were hit as well. More than $700 million in crypto positions were liquidated in the 24 hours before the latest drop, and about 86% were bets on higher prices. The slide below $60,000 likely forced out more of them.
The move extends a month-long slump. Bitcoin has dropped roughly $20,000 in the past month, a slide tracked as the price fell under $62,000 on Thursday.

Crypto stocks fell even faster. Strategy (MSTR) was down about 7% near $79.85, a day after it tumbled for a sixth straight session . Coinbase (COIN) fell about 3% to $105.36. Shares of Strive (ASST) fell to $15.31 Friday morning, down 21.47%, or $4.19, over the past five days. The stock has slid steadily from near $19.50 as bitcoin price’s sell-off deepened, with its sharpest drop in Friday’s trading.
Bitcoin miners took the worst of it. MARA Holdings (MARA) dropped about 11% to $5.55. Riot Platforms (RIOT) lost about 11% to $15.85, and CleanSpark (CLSK) fell about 12% to $5.13.

Data center operators that also mine bitcoin were hit hard. IREN fell about 12% to $12.62, and Cipher Digital (CIFR) dropped 14% to $5.58. Both have traded with AI stocks, which are also under pressure.
The bitcoin price is now at its lowest since the first days of July. Bitcoin set its record above $126,000 in October 2025, so it has lost more than half its value from that peak.
At the time of writing, the bitcoin price is near $59,600.

extraction.body: On November 16, 2026, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office for Civil Rights (OCR) announced a final rule amending the HIPAA Privacy Rule, which was published in the Federal Register on November 19, 2026. The rule finalizes much, but far from all, of OCR's January 2021 proposed rule. The proposed rule grew out of HHS' 2018 "Regulatory Sprint to Coordinated Care," which turned out to be more of a limp to the finish line. The final rule takes effect January 19, 2027, and regulated entities generally must comply by July 19, 2027, except that they have until January 18, 2028, to make any necessary revisions to business associate agreements (BAAs) if the BAAs are not renewed or modified sooner. The bulk of the final rule addresses an individual's right to access their protected health information (PHI), which has been a focus of OCR enforcement for years. The changes will require most covered entities to revisit their access policies, procedures, and workflows. Covered entities still may require that access requests be in writing, but the rule clarifies that "in writing" means that "the request itself serves as documentation of the individual's exercise of the right of access, including when the request is submitted electronically or on paper." 45 C.F.R. § 164.524(b)(1)(ii). OCR's message elevates function over form: a covered entity may not reject an otherwise clear request because the individual did not use the entity's preferred form or format. The current 30-day deadline is replaced with "[a]s soon as practicable, but no later than 15 calendar days after receipt of the request." OCR retained a single 30-day extension, rather than shortening it to 15 days as proposed. Discussions with the individual about the scope, format, or other aspects of a request do not extend the deadline. And if another federal or state law imposes a shorter deadline, that shorter timeframe is what is "practicable," effectively folding stricter state access deadlines into HIPAA compliance. OCR did not finalize its proposal to require a policy for prioritizing urgent requests. Consistent with Ciox Health, LLC v. Azar , the "right of access to direct"—an individual's right to have a covered entity send their PHI to a third party—is limited to electronic copies of PHI in an electronic health record (EHR). It does not apply to paper copies or to PHI in a designated record set maintained outside the EHR. The same 15-day standard applies to these requests. OCR did not finalize its proposal to require covered health care providers to respond to oral requests to direct records to a designated person. Notably, a personal health application is not treated as a third party. The rule defines a personal health application as an electronic application used by an individual to access health information about that individual, which can be drawn from multiple sources, provided that the information is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual—and not by or primarily for a covered entity or primarily for another person. A request to send PHI to a personal health application is treated as the equivalent of sending the PHI to the individual, rather than an exercise of the right of access to direct, and is not limited to electronic copies of PHI in an EHR. Despite the name, the definition is not limited to "apps" but also includes, for example, websites for managing health information. The rule clarifies that if a requested form and format is readily producible—including because another federal or state law requires a covered entity to implement technology that has the effect of making PHI available in that form and format—the covered entity must provide the PHI in that form and format. Depending on the individual's request and the covered entity's capabilities, that may require mailing PHI, emailing it, or transmitting it to the individual's personal health application if the PHI is readily producible in that manner. A covered entity that offers a summary of PHI in lieu of a copy must inform the individual that they retain the right to access their PHI, including the right of access to direct, if they do not agree to receive the summary. The rule narrows what a covered entity may charge for access. Fees may include only labor for copying PHI into electronic or non-electronic form, supplies for non-electronic copies, postage and shipping for non-electronic copies, and preparing an explanation or summary of PHI. Fees may not include electronic media (such as a USB drive) or postage for shipping electronic media. Covered entities may not charge for inspection of PHI or for electronic access through an internet-based method that does not involve labor costs for copying, such as through a personal health application. OCR did not finalize its proposal to require individualized fee estimates upon request. Covered entities also must post a fee schedule on their website (if they have one) and make it available in paper or electronic form, at the point of service, or at an office that is responsible for releasing medical records and, as applicable, to provide fee schedule information verbally (e.g., over the telephone). The fee schedule must identify all types of access available free of charge, standard fees for electronic and non-electronic copies under the right of access, and standard fees for copies disclosed pursuant to an authorization. That last item means the new requirement reaches beyond the right of access, and covered entities that rely on release-of-information vendors will need to coordinate with those vendors on the content of the schedule. The rule prohibits covered entities from imposing unreasonable verification measures that cause an individual to expend unnecessary effort or resources when a less burdensome measure is practicable for the covered entity. The rule replaces several commas with semicolons in the definition of "health care operations," so that "population-based activities relating to improving health or reducing health care costs," "protocol development," and "case management and care coordination" each stand alone. The change clarifies that individual-level case management and care coordination—including by health plans—qualify as health care operations, rather than only population-based activities. The rule also expressly permits a covered entity to disclose PHI to a social services agency, community-based organization, home and community-based services provider, or similar third party that provides health or human services to specific individuals, for individual-level care coordination and case management activities, whether those activities constitute treatment or health care operations. However, OCR did not finalize a proposed exception to the minimum necessary standard for these disclosures, so covered entities will still need to make reasonable efforts to limit disclosures for health care operations to the minimum necessary. In what may be the most welcome change for health care providers, the rule eliminates the requirement for a covered health care provider with a direct treatment relationship to make a good faith effort to obtain a written acknowledgment of receipt of the NPP. There have been frequent stories of patients believing that the acknowledgment form is some sort of consent, and registration staff refusing to admit patients who do not sign the form. The bad news is that covered entities will need to revise their NPPs again, following the February 2026 updates for substance use disorder records (see our prior advisory ). passages: The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans.
Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips.
The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit.
That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher.

extraction.body: The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips? The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue. Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research , some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024. But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision. That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers. However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue. Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space. Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts. That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale. extraction.body: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.” Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely). The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote: Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside. Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls. Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary. As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible. Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote: The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request. This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models. The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it. The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon. Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms.

sources.title: California AG subpoenas Nvidia over worries about Huang’s ties with China
passages: California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy.

The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen).

Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors.
In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal.
“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote.
Huang has agreed to testify before Congress after several senior lawmakers threatened to subpoena him.

extraction.body: California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy. The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public. “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement . “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added. The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen). The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position. The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government. The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors. Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote. extraction.body: California’s Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday evening said the state has served an investigative subpoena to Nvidia following news of former CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman who the U.S. government believes is a Chinese spy. The state is investigating the company to find out if its advanced GPUs or confidential information may have been shared with China, and if the company had somehow misled its investors and the public. “The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” Bonta said in a statement . “My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information — and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law,” he added. The investigation comes in the wake of a messy couple of weeks for Nvidia, which has overnight come under intense scrutiny around the world due to the implications of Huang’s alleged relationship with the Chinese national, Alice Huang (who is not related to Jensen). The Nvidia founder resigned last week after further revelations of extramarital affairs with the company’s employees. And while many tech voices have been petitioning Nvidia to bring back Huang as CEO, saying they see him as indispensable to the further development of the AI industry, the company’s new chair, Harvey Jones, said earlier this week that Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Huang to his position. The company’s board has hired a law firm as well as an independent slate of directors to investigate the extent of the damage, and the U.S. government is trying to find out the extent of Alice Huang’s ties with the Chinese government. The U.S. Congress is also gearing up to subpoena Huang, seeking questions about the affair, and the SEC is said to be launching a civil probe into the company, trying to find out if Nvidia’s public disclosures could have misled investors. Democratic representatives have also opened an inquiry into the Trump administration’s management of Nvidia’s chip sales to China. In a scathing letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Democrats last week asked the Commerce Department to preserve records about an arrangement that they called questionable and illegal. “Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors,” Bonta wrote. extraction.body: Apple, Google, and Microsoft called out for failing to provide developers with adequate AI agent controls Signal, the encrypted messaging app, has barred Google Gemini, Apple Siri, and other AI agents from accessing messages unless the user has explicitly granted permission, based on privacy concerns. Citing the screenshot blocking implemented last year to defend against Microsoft Recall, Signal CEO Meredith Whittaker said similar measures have become necessary to prevent agentic software available in iOS and Android from gaining access to communication that's intended to be private. "Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems," wrote Whittaker in a blog post . "In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents 'scan' the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding." The result is that private messages ingested by these agentic systems may end up on someone else's server where they're no longer private. Updates to Signal's iOS and Android apps now include controls that by default block Siri on iOS and Gemini and other agents on Android from taking screenshots, which AI agents process using optical character recognition to extract text. Whittaker says that those who wish to take screenshots of their messages can disable this protection via Signal's settings menu, but warns doing so risks exposing your Signal content (and that sent by your contacts) to AI agents. Screenshot blocking, Whittaker concedes, is only a partial solution since AI agents may have other ways to access application data through the device file system. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy," she said. "Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS." Apple is taking some action to implement protection from AI agents on macOS, though it appears to be doing so largely to defend against third-party access to data rather than to limit its own Siri service. Siri can be turned off separately. With macOS 27.3 , currently in public beta testing, Apple's desktop operating system will get more granular controls on two APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. The result will be more permission prompts for users of macOS apps that seek access to user data, and the inconvenience of applying for an entitlement from Apple to obtain Full Disk Access for backup software and assistive technologies that use Accessibility APIs. "As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially," Apple said when it introduced the Full Disk Access change. "We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy." Apple is also reportedly working on its own AI agent in a bid to compete with Anthropic and OpenAI. It remains to be seen whether Apple will use its operating system ownership as competitive leverage against AI firms that threaten its gatekeeping power, as it has done with web browsers . While Apple casts itself as an ally that's helping to defend device customers against prying AI agents, Signal's decision to block Siri shows that AI agents have complicated trust decisions and the competitive landscape. AI agents are supposed to serve the user but when they spirit data away to the cloud and come between customers and merchants, they wear out their welcome. AI agents also threaten the business relationship between consumers and merchants. Amazon has blocked shopping agents like Meta Muse from its e-commerce site (though not AWS Marketplace ) while Walmart has invited third-party agents to interact through its AI Gateway. Anthropic has blocked subscription customers from using third-party harnesses . United Airlines has banned transactions from unauthorized AI bots. Similar barriers or limitations related to third-party AI agents have been erected by Target, Home Depot, Etsy, eBay, JPMorgan Chase, Charles Schwab, Citigroup, and Wells Fargo, among others. Meanwhile, there's a burgeoning industry in bot detection and mitigation, led by the likes of Cloudflare, Akamai, and DataDome, to name a few. The web browser is sometimes referred to as a user agent, based on the idealistic notion that it serves its user. That vision has been muddied by online advertising and data collection, and default settings that often serve the interests of browser makers instead of promoting privacy. Now AI agents face the same scrutiny as people wonder whether their agents really serve them or someone else. sources.body: From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace.

extraction.body: Tech companies are racing to figure out how AI can make everyday work a little easier. From notetakers to webcams that follow your movements, here are six AI-powered gadgets worth checking out if you want to upgrade your workspace. If you’re constantly scribbling notes during meetings, the Flowtica Scribe could save you from having to type everything up afterward. The AI-powered pen combines traditional handwriting with audio recording. You can use its built-in gel pen to take notes, tap the side to highlight important points, and press the end of the pen to start recording audio. Once the meeting is over, its AI can transcribe the conversation, summarize key takeaways, and create a to-do list based on what was discussed. You can even ask the AI questions about the meeting to find specific information without having to go through the entire recording. The Scribe comes with a built-in microphone and 32GB of onboard storage. It can also identify up to 15 different speakers and supports 92 languages. Anker’s AI-powered recording pin, Soundcore Work , is designed to capture conversations, meetings, and quick voice memos without taking up much space on your desk. Priced at $159 (currently reduced to $99 in the Amazon Black Friday sale), the coin-sized device comes with a puck-shaped charging case and can record for up to eight hours on a single charge, extending to 32 hours when used with its case. Anker also claims a recording range of up to 5 meters, making it useful for capturing conversations around a meeting table. If you need more recording capacity or access to additional AI features, Anker offers optional subscription plans, including Pro ($99 per year) and Unlimited ($239 per year). Logitech’s MX Keypad brings AI shortcuts directly to your desk, with dedicated buttons that let you launch your preferred AI assistant or trigger specific productivity tools with a single press. If you frequently switch between different apps and AI assistants, having these shortcuts within reach could make your workday easier. The keypad can be configured to work with tools such as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code, along with a range of popular productivity and creative apps, such as OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Teams, PowerPoint, Excel, Notion, Slack, Photoshop, Final Cut Pro, Zoom, and Figma. Amazon’s Kindle Scribe Colorsoft brings color to the company’s digital notetaking lineup and offers some neat AI features designed to clean up your messy notes. Starting at $479 , the device is aimed at people who regularly work with digital documents, including students, researchers, and professionals who prefer annotating files rather than printing them out. It lets you highlight important passages, mark up documents, organize handwritten notes, and sketch out ideas. Notably, the Scribe Colorsoft incorporates AI-powered tools to clean up messy handwriting, straighten highlighting and underlining, summarize notes, and help turn scattered thoughts into more organized information. Its search feature can look across your saved notes to find specific details and help identify connections between different entries. If you’re tired of adjusting your webcam during video calls, Insta360’s Link 2 Pro aims to take care of that for you. Priced at $249 (discounted to $199 for Black Friday ), this AI-powered webcam combines 4K video capture with intelligent tracking and automatic framing. Its smart video tracker can follow your movements and adjust the camera’s position to keep you in view, even when you move around your workspace, which is particularly useful for people who regularly give presentations, teach online, or switch between sitting at their desk and standing during video calls. The camera also offers group tracking, which can come in handy during team meetings or presentations involving multiple people. AI-powered noise cancellation is another useful addition, helping reduce distracting background sounds during calls. Your desk could probably use a little intelligence, too. Autonomous Desk Pro is an adjustable standing desk designed to encourage healthier habits throughout the workday. Beyond switching between sitting and standing positions, the AI-powered desk uses built-in sensors to monitor your activity and remind you when it’s time to move, stretch, or change positions. It can track how much time you spend sitting versus standing, giving you a better idea of your daily work habits. The AI features go a step further by allowing you to ask questions about your activity. For example, you can check how long you’ve been sitting, compare your activity with the previous day, or get information about the room’s CO2 levels to help determine whether it’s time to open a window. extraction.body: A new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch can make a great holiday gift, but they can also take a pretty big dent out of your budget. That’s especially true this year, as rising hardware prices have made MacBooks and other Apple devices even more expensive. Fortunately, Black Friday offers a chance to save, especially since great deals are already available on a wide range of Apple devices. Some discounts even extend to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro, which have dropped to new lows. Most of the discounts below are promoted as Black Friday deals, but we’ve also included a few that aren’t technically part of the shopping event but have “coincidentally” dropped in price in the last week or so. Black Friday isn’t until November 27th, however, so some prices could fall further in the coming days. Apple is also kicking off its own Black Friday shopping event that day, offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases. That said, if you don’t want to wait, we think the deals below are already worth taking advantage of. Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review. * The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon, which is $19 shy of their best price to date (Best Buy and Target also have them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. Amazon also has the pink headphones on sale for $79.99, while other colors are $20 more at both retailers. The headphones are a noticeable improvement over their predecessor, delivering more detailed sound and support for lossless audio. Read our review. * The Beats Studio Buds Plus are down to around $89.95 ($80 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target, nearly matching their lowest price to date. The redesigned laptop is Apple’s first with an OLED touchscreen, which allows for rich colors and deep blacks. Apple’s newest entry-level smartwatch remains our top recommendation for anyone who wants a basic fitness tracker, as it offers all the essentials alongside an always-on display and Apple’s S10 chip, which enables on-device Siri requests. It has a smaller screen and a slower chip than the newer model, and it lacks an OLED screen, the Acoustic Display, and water resistance. Still, it’s a great option for reading and everyday use that’s currently more affordable than its $699 successor, with support for Apple Intelligence and the Apple Pencil Pro.

extraction.body: The push to build data centers in space faces plenty of obstacles, from tricky engineering to a dearth of rockets that could take chips to orbit. But what about paying for the chips? The data center ecosystem currently depends on debt financing, with cloud providers borrowing to build out data centers and then paying back the loans with a share of the revenue. Those deals typically use the chips as collateral — if the data centers default on their loans, the lenders can take possession of the chips and resell them. That backstop makes it cheaper for companies to finance their chips. Even older chips retain value — according to Compute Credit Index Research , some H100s are selling for about half of their original cost basis from 2023, while some H200 configurations are selling for the same price they did when introduced in 2024. But you’re not going to repossess chips installed in a satellite orbiting 300 miles above Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. The Financial Times is reporting that lenders behind SpaceX’s $40 billion chip financing deal asked that none of the chips purchased be used for the company’s orbital data center plans. It’s not clear if they succeeded in getting SpaceX to agree with the provision. That may not matter to the company in the near term — SpaceX’s ability to deploy compute at terrestrial ground stations has proven lucrative, and on the company’s most recent earnings call, CEO Elon Musk detailed how he was dispatching engineers from the company’s rocket team to accelerate that build-out by taking on challenges like casting turbine blades for generators at faster than existing suppliers. However, open questions remain about how easy it will be to find land and power to support the data center build-out. Many potential projects face delays and local opposition, while markets wait to see the state of compute demand and the ability of its buyers to turn it into revenue. Musk, meanwhile, began saying at the beginning of 2026 that he believes space will be the “cheapest” place to operate data centers in two to three years. That’s unlikely until SpaceX can fly its Starship rocket in a fully reusable configuration. In its most recent flight test, the company failed to recover the booster stage but did succeed in landing the orbital stage of the rocket back at its launch facility in Texas. It’s not clear, though, when the second stage will fly again or how expensive it will be to prepare it for a second trip to space. Even with Starship, however, SpaceX — as well as startups like StarCloud, Cowboy Space Corporation, Sophia Space, Orbital, and others — will need to buy chips. If the already daunting economics of space data centers weren’t challenging enough, it looks like they’ll be spending more to buy them than their terrestrial counterparts. That might be an advantage for Google, which is focused on deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher. SpaceX and Tesla are working together to build their own chip foundry, Terafab, in the U.S., but that project has yet to break ground and will require years and billions of dollars before it starts producing semiconductors at scale.
