extraction.body: Test using prompts with unique, trackable secrets proves that data doesn’t stay private. Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible. “We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.” Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely). The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote: Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside. Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls. Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary. As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible. Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote: The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request. This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models. The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it. The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday . “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”

Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).
The most concerning finding was the breach of three separate hosting providers. The attackers who compromised one of the providers reused “a couple hundred” of the AWS keys. Moore wrote:

Each key was sent in exactly one request to one provider, all within a few short windows in late October, and every request we sent during those windows was stolen. Some of the stolen keys came from requests that the provider rejected before a model ever ran—this tells us that the attacker was copying requests at the provider’s front door, and not somewhere deeper in the inference stack. In the other two breaches, some of the stolen requests were marked as ZDR. A privacy flag doesn’t help when the attacker is already inside.

Parties tied to the hack of these three providers then tested each key, in some cases within hours of being seeded, to see what kind of resources it gave access to. The parties looked through S3 buckets, secrets managers, and parameter stores in search of still more credentials. They also tried to enable hosted models in AWS Bedrock and added their own IAM users to maintain access. In all, the stolen bait keys were used “tens of thousands” of times in AWS API calls.

Secrets sent to two of the hacked providers were quickly used together, almost immediately, from the same rented server. That means the providers were almost certainly compromised by the same adversary.

As noted earlier, some of the secrets were stolen by the resellers themselves. To lure prompts to their servers, they offered low prices. Then they turned on request logging and waited. Moore identified them by sending requests to the same model through different sellers. When credentials were later reused when sent through one seller and not another, the researcher knew it was the reseller, not the model provider, that was responsible.
Last, the canary experiment revealed that some providers are scraping secret URLs put into the prompts, in violation of privacy terms. Moore wrote:

The clearest example involves a Chinese AI lab. This lab’s systems fetched the secret URLs from more than half of the prompts that we sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked as “no data collection” or Zero Data Retention. The scraper typically showed up two or three days after the request.

This wasn’t limited to requests sent to the lab directly. Several US hosting providers resell this lab’s models, and prompts sent to those providers triggered the exact same scraper—the prompts were flowing back to the lab. A customer who picked a US provider specifically to keep their data in the U.S. didn’t get what they paid for. Later on, a git client on a different cloud started trying to clone the private repositories referenced in our prompts, but only for prompts that used this lab’s models.

The researcher said he found one US hosting provider crawling a secret URL more than two months after it was used in a single inference call to its search endpoint. Another ran a scraper that came back for URLs days after each request, regardless of the AI router used to reach it.

The blockbuster research is the latest indictment exposing the lax privacy and security that’s endemic in much of the AI ecosystem. The findings mean that people who want to ensure secrets they put into prompts stay private face a daunting task that isn’t likely to become easier any time soon.

Lenders backing a $43 billion debt deal for Elon Musk -led Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) are reportedly trying to stop the company from sending valuable Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) AI chips into space, fearing they could lose the assets securing their loans.

Lenders fear they may not recover or resell the semiconductors if SpaceX launches them into space and subsequently defaults, the Financial Times reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the discussions.
SpaceX says the financed chips will operate on Earth, and it remains unclear whether lenders secured the proposed restriction.

passages: Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.
SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth.

But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.
Bondholders want SpaceX’s valuable chip collateral kept on Earth and within reach.

Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers. The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips. SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter. It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents. The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating. The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class. SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips. The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people said. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday. The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added. More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco. Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment. Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX. SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s. Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus. The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease. “The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” said Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management. “This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he said. Additional reporting by Jill R Shah in New York.

But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.
It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.
The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.

The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.

SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.

The debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people said. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.
The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.

Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

SpaceX plans to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.
Moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.
The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.

“The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” said Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.
“This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he said.

passages: U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, and Kyiv’s European allies expressed concerns about President Trump’s meeting in China with the Kremlin leader.

“And I think that that comes with at least what the Russians are saying, which is their intention is when this war is over to not have another war in the future.” Kushner said Trump is “open” to an Article 5-like security guarantee for Ukraine, although “obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that.
It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, and whether Russia and Ukraine would ultimately accept them.

Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said Russia will need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where “our drones are waiting for the cargo.” The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday its defenses intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions during the night.

extraction.body: U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Thursday he believes Russia is “comfortable” with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, and Kyiv’s European allies expressed concerns about President Trump’s meeting in China with the Kremlin leader. President Vladimir Putin, meanwhile, vowed to retaliate against Ukraine for the “serious damage” it caused with three aerial attacks this week on the vital Kerch Bridge, which links illegally occupied Crimea with the Russian mainland. “We will respond to these attacks, and I want everyone to be clear about that,” Putin told reporters in Shenzhen, China, where he attended the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. Kushner and fellow U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff were in Berlin to reassure nearly 40 European leaders about Trump's discussions on ending the nearly five-year war at his trilateral talks with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Ukraine has long sought entry into NATO, particularly for its common defense guarantee under the alliance's Article 5, in which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all. It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, and whether Russia and Ukraine would ultimately accept them. The Berlin meeting was convened to explore Ukraine's postwar security arrangements with Kyiv's European backers. President Volodymyr Zelensky wants to ensure that Russia doesn’t invade again, and Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders. “I think we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5,” Kushner said. “And I think that that comes with at least what the Russians are saying, which is their intention is when this war is over to not have another war in the future.” Kushner said Trump is “open” to an Article 5-like security guarantee for Ukraine, although “obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that. And we also have to make sure that it’s part of a broader security package.” He stressed that Trump wants to make a deal with Europe “by his side,” and is not looking to impose a unilateral agreement. "Any deal we do will be in close consultation with Ukraine and with Europe. And that’s something that he also asked us to come here today and reassure people in that regard,” said Kushner, who is Trump's son-in-law. He and Witkoff have led Trump administration efforts to end the war that followed Russia’s all-out invasion of Ukraine. The most recent talks in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week yielded no major breakthrough. Trump called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, according to Kushner. Thursday's Berlin meeting came hours after the latest attack on the Kerch Bridge by Ukraine. The strikes have seriously damaged the 12-mile bridge over the Kerch Strait that links the Black and Azov seas. The span is vital to sustaining Russia’s military operations. The bridge is a potent reminder of Russia’s illegal annexation of the Crimean peninsula and has been a prime target for Ukraine. Train traffic stopped after the overnight strike while authorities assessed the damage, but it resumed in the afternoon, according to Russian state news agency RIA Novosti. The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Putin as he met in China with Xi and Trump, as well as to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable. In China, Putin insisted the bridge is a civilian asset, adding that he had ordered it closed to carrying military hardware or ammunition. Putin also said that the road side of the bridge had been “seriously damaged” but vowed to rebuild it. The rail section, which runs parallel to the road, is believed to be stronger in order to bear the greater weight of cargo transport. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said Russia will need to reroute fuel and ammunition supplies over land, where “our drones are waiting for the cargo.” The Russian Defense Ministry said Thursday its defenses intercepted 53 Ukrainian drones over 10 Russian regions during the night. A Ukrainian attack on Russia’s Saratov region killed three people and wounded two others, local Gov. Roman Busargin said, and a drone killed a woman traveling by bicycle with her 8-year-old grandson in the Bryansk region, Gov. Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations. Explosions and sirens rang out across Kyiv during the day, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies sustained minor damage, officials said. Two people, including a 44-year-old woman, were killed and at least 23 people, including a 12-year-old boy, were reported wounded as Russian strikes caused damage in 12 regions. Russia’s bigger army hopes to exhaust Ukraine on the front line through sheer weight of numbers in terms of soldiers, armor and weapons. But Kyiv’s defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances. Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine’s resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv’s domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries. In China, Trump called Putin “my friend.” The American president’s relationship with Zelensky has soured recently, although the question of U.S. support for Ukraine could be raised by Democrats who will take control of Congress in January after their wins in the midterm elections. European leaders have tried to isolate Putin diplomatically and have heavily sanctioned the Russian economy as they fear being sidelined by Trump’s direct talks with Putin.

passages: U.S. envoy Jared Kushner has said Russia may accept NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine, adding that President Donald Trump wants to bring an end to Russia's full-scale invasion "with Europe by his side."

"I think we've got the Russians comfortable with that concept where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5," Kushner said alongside European leaders at a news conference in Germany on Thursday, referring to the part of NATO's treaty that enshrines the principle of collective defense.
It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, or whether Russia or Ukraine would accept them.
Russia's Foreign Ministry, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry and NATO were not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC on Friday morning.
Ukraine has long held ambitions to join the alliance.
Russia has previously said that if Kyiv joined NATO, it would cause problems for many years.
Russia launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on Ukraine's energy and transport infrastructure overnight, damaging three bridges in Kyiv and killing at least three people, authorities said.
They have led the Trump administration's efforts to end Russia's nearly five-year-long war with Ukraine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Tuesday described it as an "unprecedented operation" several weeks in the making, with Ukraine's defense forces, security services and weapons manufacturers involved.

His comments come shortly after Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held historic trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a meeting that did not appear to result in any concessions on Ukraine or European security.

sources.title: Kushner says Russia is 'comfortable' with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end war after Trump talks with Putin - PBS
passages: BERLIN (AP) — U.S. envoy Jared Kushner on Thursday said Russia is "comfortable" with NATO-like security guarantees for Ukraine to end the war as it nears the five-year mark.

The attack came hours before the start of talks in Berlin between Kushner, Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort and fear being sidelined by Trump's direct talks with Putin.

Kushner and Witkoff have led Trump administration efforts to end nearly five years of war following Russia's all-out invasion of its neighbor and recently have mediated new discussions, though the talks have yielded no major breakthrough.
The American leader called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said.
The meeting will also explore how Ukraine's European backers can fit into postwar security arrangements.
Kyiv wants to ensure that Russia doesn't invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders.

The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops.
It is a potent reminder of Russia's illegal annexation of the territory and has been a prime target for Ukraine.
Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations.
Explosions and sirens rang out across Kyiv during the day, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies sustained minor damage, officials said.
Another American envoy, Steve Witkoff, said U.S.
President Donald Trump discussed Ukraine and a peaceful end to the war during his trilateral talks with the Russian and Chinese leaders earlier Thursday.

The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and Trump, as well as to demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.

Kushner said Thursday on X that Washington's priority at Thursday's meeting in Berlin is to "further strengthen our close coordination with Ukraine and Europe, work toward a unified position on the key elements of a lasting peace, and to jointly prepare the agenda and proposed format for the next round of multilateral negotiations."
Russia's bigger army hopes to exhaust Ukraine on the front line through sheer weight of numbers in terms of soldiers, armor and weapons.
But Kyiv's defenses are largely holding the Russians back, sapping Russian momentum with the help of drones that quickly choke off troop advances.

Russia has resorted to strategic bombing to wear down Ukraine's resistance, placing special emphasis on knocking out power ahead of winter, while Kyiv's domestically developed long-range drones and missiles have struck deep inside Russia, often targeting its oil refineries.
In China, Trump called Putin "my friend." The American president's relationship with Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has soured.
Ukrainian officials fear their country's fate could be determined by agreements between Trump and Putin, while European governments are alarmed by Moscow's aggression.

It was not immediately clear what form potential security guarantees would take, or whether Russia or Ukraine would accept them.
Russia's Foreign Ministry, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry and NATO were not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC on Friday morning.
Ukraine has long held ambitions to join the alliance.
Russia has previously said that if Kyiv joined NATO, it would cause problems for many years.

His comments come shortly after Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping held historic trilateral talks on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, a meeting that did not appear to result in any concessions on Ukraine or European security.

Kushner and Witkoff have led Trump administration efforts to end nearly five years of war following Russia's all-out invasion of its neighbor and recently have mediated new discussions, though the talks have yielded no major breakthrough.
The American leader called into the Berlin talks following his meeting with Putin, Kushner said.
The meeting will also explore how Ukraine's European backers can fit into postwar security arrangements.
Kyiv wants to ensure that Russia doesn't invade again, while Moscow wants to keep the NATO military alliance away from its borders.

The 19-kilometer (12-mile) Kerch Bridge is a key route for military and civilian supplies to Crimea, which Moscow seized in defiance of international law in 2014 and uses to support front-line troops.
It is a potent reminder of Russia's illegal annexation of the territory and has been a prime target for Ukraine.
Ukrainian authorities said that Russia launched anti-ship missiles and 98 drones at Ukraine, with hits recorded at 18 locations.
Explosions and sirens rang out across Kyiv during the day, and the Dutch and Austrian embassies sustained minor damage, officials said.

The Ukrainian strikes seemed calculated to embarrass Russian President Vladimir Putin as he met in China with President Xi Jinping and Trump, as well as to demonstrate that Kyiv still holds cards in the war and to undermine Russia's argument that its victory is inevitable.

Earlier this year, Meta settled with the attorneys general of dozens of states, some U.S. territories, and the District of Columbia over similar claims for up to $17.1 billion.

The payout could reach $3 billion, “people familiar with the matter” told Bloomberg, although it would be split between “thousands” of school districts. (If it were split equally among 3,000 districts, each would get $1 million before any deductions.) Bloomberg reported this would be the largest-ever corporate settlement with U.S. school districts. The ongoing litigation is a mass tort, which is like a class action, except the court weighs each plaintiff’s injuries and damages on an individual basis. extraction.body: Social media platforms Instagram and YouTube have a design defect which means they are addictive, a jury in the United States has ruled . The Los Angeles jury took nearly nine days to reach its verdict in the landmark case brought by a woman known as KGM against social media platforms. It awarded US$3 million in damages, with Meta (owner of Instagram) being 70% responsible and Google (owner of YouTube) 30%. The jury later awarded a further US$3 million in punitive damages. Both TikTok and Snap settled on confidential terms before the six-week trial commenced. This is Meta’s second big loss in the US courts this week, with a New Mexico jury finding the company guilty on March 24 of concealing information about the risks of child sexual exploitation and the harmful effects of its platforms on children’s mental health. KGM’s case is the first of its kind, but won’t be the last: it is one of more than 20 “bellwether” trials due to go to court soon. These are essentially test cases used to gauge juries’ reactions and set a legal precedent. As such, the verdict is set to have far reaching ripple effects. It could be big tech’s big tobacco moment, with thousands more similar cases waiting in the wings. KGM – now 20 years old – said she began using YouTube at age six and Instagram at age nine, and allegedly developed compulsive use patterns, including up to 16 hours in a single day on Instagram. The platforms’ design features, she argued, contributed to her anxiety, depression, body dysmorphia, and suicidal ideation. Her case argued that Meta and YouTube made deliberate design choices – for example, “infinite scroll” – to make their platforms more addictive to children in order to boost profits. It alleged the companies borrowed heavily from the behavioural and neurobiological techniques used by poker machines and exploited by the cigarette industry to maximise youth engagement and drive advertising revenue. These companies built machines designed to addict the brains of children, and they did it on purpose. Lanier cited an internal Meta study called “Project Myst”. This allegedly found that children who had experienced “adverse effects” were most likely to get addicted to Instagram, and that parents were powerless to stop the addiction. The moment [KGM] was locked into the machine, her mom was locked out. The jury heard that Meta’s internal communications compared the platform’s effects to pushing drugs and gambling. The jury found this internal awareness was the kind of corporate knowledge that supports liability. In addition, a YouTube memo reportedly described “viewer addiction” as a goal, and an Instagram employee wrote the company was staffed by “basically pushers”. Mark Lanier drew a direct parallel to tobacco litigation, arguing that where there is corporate knowledge, deliberate targeting, and public denial, liability follows. Meta argued KGM faced significant challenges before she ever used social media, and that the evidence did not support reducing a lifetime of hardship to a single factor. Meta’s lawyer highlighted KGM’s family dynamics as responsible for her mental health struggles, and argued social media may have actually provided a healthy outlet for her when she faced difficulties at home. Meta’s chief executive Mark Zuckerberg gave evidence for the defence: I’m not trying to maximise the amount of time people spend every month. On safety tools Meta added in recent years Zuckerberg said : I always wish we could have gotten there sooner. In closing arguments, YouTube’s lawyer argued there was not a single mention of an addiction to YouTube in KGM’s medical records. The companies centred part of their defence on Section 230 protections , arguing they cannot be held liable for content posted on their platforms. However, the judge instructed the jury that the way content is delivered is a separate consideration to what the content is. This limited Meta and Google’s ability to rely on Section 230 protections. This was one of the first cases against big tech which was a jury trial – something companies have previously been keen to avoid. For example, in June 2024, a few months ahead of a scheduled jury trial in the Department of Justice’s challenge to Google’s advertising technology monopoly, Google paid more than US$2 million (A$2.8 million) to the Department of Justice. This was treble the damages claimed, plus interest. In the US, a jury trial is only required when monetary damages are at stake. By paying the full damages amount upfront in that case, Google eliminated the damages claim and with it, the right to a jury. Until now, US courts have largely denied motions that focused on design. The effect of the jury’s verdict in KGM’s case is to demonstrate the limitations of the Section 230 protection. This is the first big tech case, on a global basis, that has examined addiction as a cause of damage. Other cases have focused on breaches of law. For example, in the case in New Mexico against Meta, the jury concluded the company made false or misleading statements and engaged in “unconscionable” trade practices that exploited children’s vulnerability and inexperience. It identified thousands of individual violations, resulting in a total penalty of US$375 million (A$539 million). KGM’s case paves the way for the many other actions seeking damages from social media platforms for the effects of addiction. There is logic for these cases to be heard concurrently in a class action in the US. The verdict could also be used as the basis for both class actions and individual actions on a global basis. Meta and Google have said separately they plan to appeal the verdict. Senior Research Associate in Media and Communications, University of Sydney Rob Nicholls is a part of the University of Sydney Centre for AI, Trust, and Governance and receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

The payout could reach $3 billion, “people familiar with the matter” told Bloomberg, although it would be split between “thousands” of school districts. The ongoing litigation is a mass tort, which is like a class action, except the court weighs each plaintiff’s injuries and damages on an individual basis. extraction.body: Social media platforms Instagram and YouTube have a design defect which means they are addictive, a jury in the United States has ruled . The Los Angeles jury took nearly nine days to reach its verdict in the landmark case brought by a woman known as KGM against social media platforms. It awarded US$3 million in damages, with Meta (owner of Instagram) being 70% responsible and Google (owner of YouTube) 30%. The jury later awarded a further US$3 million in punitive damages. Both TikTok and Snap settled on confidential terms before the six-week trial commenced. This is Meta’s second big loss in the US courts this week, with a New Mexico jury finding the company guilty on March 24 of concealing information about the risks of child sexual exploitation and the harmful effects of its platforms on children’s mental health. KGM’s case is the first of its kind, but won’t be the last: it is one of more than 20 “bellwether” trials due to go to court soon. These are essentially test cases used to gauge juries’ reactions and set a legal precedent. As such, the verdict is set to have far reaching ripple effects. It could be big tech’s big tobacco moment, with thousands more similar cases waiting in the wings. KGM – now 20 years old – said she began using YouTube at age six and Instagram at age nine, and allegedly developed compulsive use patterns, including up to 16 hours in a single day on Instagram. The platforms’ design features, she argued, contributed to her anxiety, depression, body dysmorphia, and suicidal ideation. Her case argued that Meta and YouTube made deliberate design choices – for example, “infinite scroll” – to make their platforms more addictive to children in order to boost profits. It alleged the companies borrowed heavily from the behavioural and neurobiological techniques used by poker machines and exploited by the cigarette industry to maximise youth engagement and drive advertising revenue. These companies built machines designed to addict the brains of children, and they did it on purpose. Lanier cited an internal Meta study called “Project Myst”. This allegedly found that children who had experienced “adverse effects” were most likely to get addicted to Instagram, and that parents were powerless to stop the addiction. The moment [KGM] was locked into the machine, her mom was locked out. The jury heard that Meta’s internal communications compared the platform’s effects to pushing drugs and gambling. The jury found this internal awareness was the kind of corporate knowledge that supports liability. In addition, a YouTube memo reportedly described “viewer addiction” as a goal, and an Instagram employee wrote the company was staffed by “basically pushers”. Mark Lanier drew a direct parallel to tobacco litigation, arguing that where there is corporate knowledge, deliberate targeting, and public denial, liability follows. Meta argued KGM faced significant challenges before she ever used social media, and that the evidence did not support reducing a lifetime of hardship to a single factor. Meta’s lawyer highlighted KGM’s family dynamics as responsible for her mental health struggles, and argued social media may have actually provided a healthy outlet for her when she faced difficulties at home. Meta’s chief executive Mark Zuckerberg gave evidence for the defence: I’m not trying to maximise the amount of time people spend every month. On safety tools Meta added in recent years Zuckerberg said : I always wish we could have gotten there sooner. In closing arguments, YouTube’s lawyer argued there was not a single mention of an addiction to YouTube in KGM’s medical records. The companies centred part of their defence on Section 230 protections , arguing they cannot be held liable for content posted on their platforms. However, the judge instructed the jury that the way content is delivered is a separate consideration to what the content is. This limited Meta and Google’s ability to rely on Section 230 protections. This was one of the first cases against big tech which was a jury trial – something companies have previously been keen to avoid. For example, in June 2024, a few months ahead of a scheduled jury trial in the Department of Justice’s challenge to Google’s advertising technology monopoly, Google paid more than US$2 million (A$2.8 million) to the Department of Justice. This was treble the damages claimed, plus interest. In the US, a jury trial is only required when monetary damages are at stake. By paying the full damages amount upfront in that case, Google eliminated the damages claim and with it, the right to a jury. Until now, US courts have largely denied motions that focused on design. The effect of the jury’s verdict in KGM’s case is to demonstrate the limitations of the Section 230 protection. This is the first big tech case, on a global basis, that has examined addiction as a cause of damage. Other cases have focused on breaches of law. For example, in the case in New Mexico against Meta, the jury concluded the company made false or misleading statements and engaged in “unconscionable” trade practices that exploited children’s vulnerability and inexperience. passages: Social media platforms Instagram and YouTube have a design defect which means they are addictive, a jury in the United States has ruled .

The Los Angeles jury took nearly nine days to reach its verdict in the landmark case brought by a woman known as KGM against social media platforms. It awarded US$3 million in damages, with Meta (owner of Instagram) being 70% responsible and Google (owner of YouTube) 30%. The jury later awarded a further US$3 million in punitive damages.
Both TikTok and Snap settled on confidential terms before the six-week trial commenced.

This is Meta’s second big loss in the US courts this week, with a New Mexico jury finding the company guilty on March 24 of concealing information about the risks of child sexual exploitation and the harmful effects of its platforms on children’s mental health.

KGM’s case is the first of its kind, but won’t be the last: it is one of more than 20 “bellwether” trials due to go to court soon. These are essentially test cases used to gauge juries’ reactions and set a legal precedent.
As such, the verdict is set to have far reaching ripple effects. It could be big tech’s big tobacco moment, with thousands more similar cases waiting in the wings.

KGM – now 20 years old – said she began using YouTube at age six and Instagram at age nine, and allegedly developed compulsive use patterns, including up to 16 hours in a single day on Instagram. The platforms’ design features, she argued, contributed to her anxiety, depression, body dysmorphia, and suicidal ideation.

Her case argued that Meta and YouTube made deliberate design choices – for example, “infinite scroll” – to make their platforms more addictive to children in order to boost profits. It alleged the companies borrowed heavily from the behavioural and neurobiological techniques used by poker machines and exploited by the cigarette industry to maximise youth engagement and drive advertising revenue.
These companies built machines designed to addict the brains of children, and they did it on purpose.

Lanier cited an internal Meta study called “Project Myst”. This allegedly found that children who had experienced “adverse effects” were most likely to get addicted to Instagram, and that parents were powerless to stop the addiction.
The moment [KGM] was locked into the machine, her mom was locked out.

The jury heard that Meta’s internal communications compared the platform’s effects to pushing drugs and gambling. The jury found this internal awareness was the kind of corporate knowledge that supports liability.
In addition, a YouTube memo reportedly described “viewer addiction” as a goal, and an Instagram employee wrote the company was staffed by “basically pushers”.
Mark Lanier drew a direct parallel to tobacco litigation, arguing that where there is corporate knowledge, deliberate targeting, and public denial, liability follows.
Meta argued KGM faced significant challenges before she ever used social media, and that the evidence did not support reducing a lifetime of hardship to a single factor.

Meta’s lawyer highlighted KGM’s family dynamics as responsible for her mental health struggles, and argued social media may have actually provided a healthy outlet for her when she faced difficulties at home.
Meta’s chief executive Mark Zuckerberg gave evidence for the defence:
I’m not trying to maximise the amount of time people spend every month.

I always wish we could have gotten there sooner.
In closing arguments, YouTube’s lawyer argued there was not a single mention of an addiction to YouTube in KGM’s medical records.

This was treble the damages claimed, plus interest.

In the US, a jury trial is only required when monetary damages are at stake. By paying the full damages amount upfront in that case, Google eliminated the damages claim and with it, the right to a jury.
Until now, US courts have largely denied motions that focused on design.
The effect of the jury’s verdict in KGM’s case is to demonstrate the limitations of the Section 230 protection.

sources.title: Bitcoin suffered identical sell-off pattern ahead of Anthropic, SpaceX IPOs — what happens next? - CNBC
passages: Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.
The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing.
"Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC.
"The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display.
Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market."
Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations.
Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next.
With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

"[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm.
Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole.

Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.

The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing. Ether declined 25.3% in the 30 days preceding Anthropic's debut, and 28% in the same window ahead of SpaceX. "Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC. "The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display. Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market." "Stores of value function as such over long horizons, but in the short term are still liquidity driven," Sheffield said. "We saw this in early Covid when the market fled to cash. Stock, bonds, commodities ... it didn't matter, you were being sold for cash." While investors appear to be rotating capital out of crypto to make room for history-making IPO investments, that can't be said with precise certainty. Crypto has also been under pressure from ETF outflows, leverage, macro uncertainty and broader risk-off sentiment. Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next. With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns. "[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm. "My view is that [for] bitcoin, the most likely scenario is that it chops around here." The expiration of IPO allocation restrictions can influence the timing of capital flows into digital assets, Sheffield said. "Post SpaceX we saw the wealth effect in full force," Sheffield said. "Many brokers make traders wait 15-30 days before they are allowed to flip shares they received as allocations. … If you went long ETH versus SpaceX on the day of the IPO, on day 31 was when you would have become profitable." Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000. As of Friday, bitcoin was hovering at the upper end of a critical $60,000 to $62,000 support range. Its next move could determine whether it can stabilize or if it will face another leg lower and revisit its July low of $57,737.35. Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations. The declines began in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand. Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole. Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said. "Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite." "The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. "Anytime anyone's been around early spring, what you notice is it gets really cold still, it still rains – it's not necessarily great weather, and I think that's the environment we're in for bitcoin." passages: Bitcoin’s latest price decline is drawing comparisons with its pre-SpaceX IPO correction, raising speculation that history could repeat as Anthropic makes its public-market debut.
$BTC has dropped toward $62,000 after a sharp sell-off, closely mirroring the weakness seen before SpaceX’s IPO earlier this year.
After SpaceX went public in June, $BTC staged a short-term rebound, climbing from around $63,000 toward $66,000 over the following days.
Anthropic’s IPO has become a major market event, with the company pricing shares at $83, raising approximately $81.3 billion through its public offering.
Bitcoin has declined nearly 28% from its September peak near $87,400, with selling pressure intensifying ahead of Anthropic’s November 19 debut.

passages: Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol 'ANT' on the 19th (local time).
The company announced that it completed both its public and private offerings on the 20th.
The public offering consisted of 1.127 billion shares at $83 per share, totaling approximately $93.5 billion.
Including the private placement, the total funding reached approximately $119.5 billion.
According to CNBC, Bitcoin's price fell 22.7% in the 30 days prior to the Anthropic listing, and it dropped 22.3% in the month leading up to the SpaceX listing on June 12th.
Ethereum also saw similar selling pressure in the cryptocurrency market ahead of the two major IPOs, declining 25.3% and 28% during the respective periods.
He views Bitcoin as being in the early stages of forming a bottom and believes the market is likely to repeat fluctuations for the time being.
The timing of when lock-up periods on IPO-allocated shares expire could also impact capital flows.

The SpaceX IPO documentation includes a structure where share sale restrictions vary by existing shareholder, and some holdings become eligible for trading in stages following future earnings releases.
Analysts suggest that when large IPOs occur, the correlation across asset markets can rise sharply as investors sell existing assets to buy newly listed stocks.

Matthew Sheffield, Chief Investment Officer at Sharplink, cited the simultaneous sell-off of tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, and cryptocurrencies during the first 15 minutes of Anthropic's listing as an example of such capital movement.
He noted that even assets that function as stores of value in the long term are influenced by cash liquidity in the short term.

Other factors cited for the recent weakness in cryptocurrency include fund outflows from exchange-traded funds, the liquidation of leveraged positions, macroeconomic uncertainty, and risk-aversion sentiment.
Nicolai Søndergaard, a research analyst at Nansen, identified $60,000 to $62,000 as the next critical test range for Bitcoin.
However, he compared Bitcoin's recovery phase to "early spring" right after the end of deep winter, explaining that sharp cold snaps and rain could still occur during the rebound process.

passages: Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year.

With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public.
As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically.

The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations.
Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention.
If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return.

What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge.

extraction.body: Bitcoin and ether just traced the same sharp sell-off pattern that preceded SpaceX's blockbuster IPO earlier this year, raising urgent questions about whether institutional money is abandoning crypto for hot tech listings. With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public. The crypto market just delivered an eerie sense of déjà vu. Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year. The correlation is raising uncomfortable questions for crypto bulls about whether institutional money views digital assets as a liquidity source to fund allocations in hot tech IPOs. As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically. The pattern matches what happened in the lead-up to SpaceX's listing, when both cryptocurrencies shed double-digit percentages before finding support only after the IPO priced. When a massive IPO looms, institutional investors appear to be liquidating portions of their crypto holdings to free up capital for new allocations. It's a liquidity rotation that hits hardest in the two to three weeks before pricing, precisely when underwriters are locking in final commitments from large buyers. Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention. But here's where it gets interesting for crypto traders. After SpaceX priced its IPO, bitcoin and ether both stabilized within days and then mounted modest recoveries over the following weeks. The theory goes that once institutional allocations are locked and IPO euphoria fades, some of that capital rotates back into crypto as investors rebalance portfolios. With Anthropic's first trading day in the books and the initial pop already priced in, crypto markets are testing whether they can find a floor. Bitcoin has shown some signs of stabilization, though trading volumes remain thin, suggesting many institutional players are still on the sidelines. What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge. That's a far cry from the narrative of bitcoin as digital gold or a portfolio hedge that trades independently of traditional markets. The institutional demand picture is murkier than it was during previous crypto rallies. While bitcoin ETFs have attracted steady inflows this year, the pace has slowed considerably. Meanwhile, the pipeline of major tech IPOs remains robust, with several AI and enterprise software unicorns reportedly preparing listings for early 2027. If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return. The key variable is whether another blockbuster IPO gets announced soon, which could trigger a repeat of the cycle. Some crypto analysts argue the sell-off is actually healthy, shaking out weak hands and establishing clearer support levels. Others worry it exposes how dependent crypto markets have become on the same institutional money that chases every hot tech trend. The difference in perspective often comes down to whether you view crypto as a mature asset class or still an emerging one fighting for legitimacy. Bitcoin is hovering near technical support levels that held during previous corrections, while ether faces a more uncertain picture given its underperformance. Trading desks report that institutional inquiry has picked up slightly since Anthropic's debut, but no one is ready to call a bottom yet. The broader implication is that crypto's fate may be more intertwined with the tech IPO calendar than many investors realized. As long as venture-backed unicorns keep going public at premium valuations, institutional investors may continue using crypto as a source of liquidity to fund those allocations. That's not necessarily bearish long-term, but it does suggest crypto markets could face periodic pressure whenever the IPO window heats up. The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations. Whether bitcoin and ether can establish a floor now that Anthropic's debut is complete will signal if the SpaceX playbook repeats, with capital gradually rotating back into digital assets. But with more AI unicorns eyeing 2027 listings, crypto investors may need to accept that their markets are now tethered to the tech IPO calendar in ways that challenge the independence narrative. The next few weeks will show if institutional demand returns or if crypto faces another cycle of liquidation as the next blockbuster listing approaches.

extraction.description: Crypto markets repeat identical sell-off seen before SpaceX listing as institutions rotate

relevantPassages.text: Bitcoin and ether both experienced sharp sell-offs in the weeks leading up to Anthropic's public debut, mirroring almost exactly the same pattern that played out before SpaceX went public earlier this year.

With Anthropic closing its first trading day up 17% at $97.17, crypto analysts are now watching to see if digital assets find a floor or if the liquidity drain deepens as more AI unicorns prepare to go public.
As Anthropic priced its IPO at $83, topping its expected range on surging institutional demand, bitcoin slid from recent highs while ether underperformed even more dramatically.

The identical sell-off pattern before both the SpaceX and Anthropic IPOs reveals an uncomfortable truth about institutional crypto holdings: they're being used as a liquidity pool to fund hot tech allocations.
Anthropic's debut certainly commanded attention.
If the SpaceX-Anthropic pattern holds, crypto investors should watch for a potential stabilization phase over the next week or two, followed by a test of whether institutional buyers return.

What makes this pattern particularly concerning for crypto advocates is that it suggests digital assets are being treated as secondary holdings, something to liquidate when "real" opportunities like AI IPOs emerge.

coreStoryFacts.text: Bitcoin has suffered nearly identical sell-offs ahead of two of the biggest public offerings this year, leaving investors wondering if competing demand for investor capital could be weighing on the cryptocurrency and perhaps delaying its recovery.
The price of the bitcoin dropped 22.7% in the 30 days before Anthropic's IPO and fell 22.3% in the month leading up to SpaceX's June 12 listing.
"Liquidity events can elevate correlations across asset classes quickly," Matthew Sheffield, chief investment officer at the ether treasury firm Sharplink , told CNBC.
"The first 15 min of [Thursday's] Anthropic IPO put that on full display.
Tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, crypto all sold off as traders sold assets to buy shares in the secondary market."
Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen.
Throughout November, bitcoin has been struggling from a combination of dollar strength, institutional selling, and ongoing leveraged bitcoin liquidations.
Still, the post-IPO price action may offer a data point in understanding where bitcoin's price goes next.
With Anthropic now public, investors are watching to see whether bitcoin and ether find a floor, and if institutional demand returns.

"[After] the SpaceX IPO, bitcoin didn't truly find its final bottom until after the IPO was completed, and it didn't actually reverse the downtrend until 70 days later," said Matt Cole, CEO and chairman of Strive Asset Management , a bitcoin treasury firm.
Bitcoin is in the early stages of forming a bottom, according to Cole.

Retail fear is elevated amid recent outages, quantum concerns and other short-term uncertainties, but bitcoin should continue to benefit from macro forces like rising debt and weakening fiat currencies, which should drive price higher, he said.
Bitcoin’s latest price decline is drawing comparisons with its pre-SpaceX IPO correction, raising speculation that history could repeat as Anthropic makes its public-market debut.
$BTC has dropped toward $62,000 after a sharp sell-off, closely mirroring the weakness seen before SpaceX’s IPO earlier this year.
After SpaceX went public in June, $BTC staged a short-term rebound, climbing from around $63,000 toward $66,000 over the following days.
Anthropic’s IPO has become a major market event, with the company pricing shares at $83, raising approximately $81.3 billion through its public offering.
Bitcoin has declined nearly 28% from its September peak near $87,400, with selling pressure intensifying ahead of Anthropic’s November 19 debut.
If history repeats, Bitcoin could see a relief rally, but the next move may not be as straightforward as bulls expect.
With Anthropic’s debut adding a fresh market catalyst, traders are now watching whether Bitcoin can stage another relief rally, or if the current sell-off has further room to run.
Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol 'ANT' on the 19th (local time).
The company announced that it completed both its public and private offerings on the 20th.
The public offering consisted of 1.127 billion shares at $83 per share, totaling approximately $93.5 billion.
Including the private placement, the total funding reached approximately $119.5 billion.
According to CNBC, Bitcoin's price fell 22.7% in the 30 days prior to the Anthropic listing, and it dropped 22.3% in the month leading up to the SpaceX listing on June 12th.

Bitcoin's next critical test is between $60,000 and $62,000, according to Nicolai Sondergaard, a research analyst at Nansen. On Friday, it was sitting at about $62,000. "Capital markets are open, … retail fears are high, and when you combine those things it's much more likely to be a dip-buying opportunity across the board, including bitcoin, than the start of a great financial crisis," said Cole. "It'll likely age as a volatile time to consider allocating to risk, not the opposite." "The winter for bitcoin is basically at the end, but after winter does not come summer, it comes early spring," he added. If history repeats, we could see another leg up after a few weeks of sideways price action. pic.twitter.com/vQpjUAxhyn The decline closely resembles Bitcoin’s movement before the SpaceX IPO in June. During that period, $BTC dropped from around $83,000 toward $59,000, marking a sharp correction ahead of the company’s public listing. The similarities have fueled speculation that investors may be reducing exposure to liquid assets ahead of major IPOs, potentially creating temporary selling pressure across crypto markets. However, the broader decline also reflects weakening risk appetite, ETF outflows, leveraged liquidations and macroeconomic uncertainty. Bitcoin’s recovery following the SpaceX IPO initially strengthened the historical comparison. After SpaceX went public in June, $BTC staged a short-term rebound, climbing from around $63,000 toward $66,000 over the following days. However, the recovery did not mark the market bottom. Bitcoin subsequently fell again, reaching a lower level later in June before beginning a broader recovery that eventually carried it toward its September high. This suggests the IPO-related pattern may involve a temporary relief rally rather than an immediate trend reversal. If the same sequence repeats, Bitcoin could recover in the short term before facing renewed selling pressure. Anthropic’s IPO has become a major market event, with the company pricing shares at $83, raising approximately $81.3 billion through its public offering. The broader transaction is expected to exceed SpaceX’s record fundraising when additional private placements are included. The listing has also coincided with a rebound in technology stocks and Nasdaq futures, improving risk appetite across financial markets. Bitcoin recovered toward $64,000 as equity futures strengthened, suggesting that sentiment surrounding the IPO could influence short-term crypto price action. However, the relationship remains uncertain. Bitcoin’s recent decline has also been driven by broader market deleveraging, institutional flows and macroeconomic concerns, meaning the IPO alone may not determine its direction. Bitcoin’s immediate recovery remains fragile after the sharp decline toward $62,000. The $62,000 zone is the critical support level. Holding above this area could allow $BTC to stabilize and attempt a recovery toward $65,000–$67,500. A sustained move above $67,500 would strengthen the short-term bullish outlook and potentially open the path toward $70,000. However, a breakdown below $62,000 could expose Bitcoin to further downside toward $59,000, followed by the $57,800 region, which represents a key previous low. Bitcoin’s pre-IPO decline has created a compelling comparison with the SpaceX listing, and Anthropic’s debut could provide a short-term catalyst for a recovery. Yet the previous cycle also showed that an initial rally can fade before the market establishes a durable bottom. Traders will therefore watch whether $BTC can hold $62,000 and regain $67,500 in the coming sessions. If history repeats, Bitcoin could see a relief rally, but the next move may not be as straightforward as bulls expect.

passages: Anthropic began trading on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker symbol 'ANT' on the 19th (local time).
The company announced that it completed both its public and private offerings on the 20th.
The public offering consisted of 1.127 billion shares at $83 per share, totaling approximately $93.5 billion.
Including the private placement, the total funding reached approximately $119.5 billion.
According to CNBC, Bitcoin's price fell 22.7% in the 30 days prior to the Anthropic listing, and it dropped 22.3% in the month leading up to the SpaceX listing on June 12th.
Ethereum also saw similar selling pressure in the cryptocurrency market ahead of the two major IPOs, declining 25.3% and 28% during the respective periods.
He views Bitcoin as being in the early stages of forming a bottom and believes the market is likely to repeat fluctuations for the time being.
The timing of when lock-up periods on IPO-allocated shares expire could also impact capital flows.

The SpaceX IPO documentation includes a structure where share sale restrictions vary by existing shareholder, and some holdings become eligible for trading in stages following future earnings releases.
Analysts suggest that when large IPOs occur, the correlation across asset markets can rise sharply as investors sell existing assets to buy newly listed stocks.

Matthew Sheffield, Chief Investment Officer at Sharplink, cited the simultaneous sell-off of tech stocks, value stocks, oil, gold, and cryptocurrencies during the first 15 minutes of Anthropic's listing as an example of such capital movement.
He noted that even assets that function as stores of value in the long term are influenced by cash liquidity in the short term.

Other factors cited for the recent weakness in cryptocurrency include fund outflows from exchange-traded funds, the liquidation of leveraged positions, macroeconomic uncertainty, and risk-aversion sentiment.
Nicolai Søndergaard, a research analyst at Nansen, identified $60,000 to $62,000 as the next critical test range for Bitcoin.
However, he compared Bitcoin's recovery phase to "early spring" right after the end of deep winter, explaining that sharp cold snaps and rain could still occur during the rebound process.

With Anthropic's first trading day in the books and the initial pop already priced in, crypto markets are testing whether they can find a floor. That's a far cry from the narrative of bitcoin as digital gold or a portfolio hedge that trades independently of traditional markets. The institutional demand picture is murkier than it was during previous crypto rallies. While bitcoin ETFs have attracted steady inflows this year, the pace has slowed considerably.
